speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In our journey towards a healthier, more resilient Singapore, we must recognise mental health not just as a component of our healthcare system but as a cornerstone of societal well-being and economic stability.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my previous addresses, I have consistently emphasised a holistic approach to health, advocating for the interconnectedness of the various health dimensions, including physical, mental and social well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we navigate modern life's complexities, it becomes increasingly apparent that mental health is not a standalone issue.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is an integral part of our daily existence, influencing our capacities to learn, work, and forge meaningful relationships.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It impacts our communities and workplaces, shaping the very heart of our nation’s productivity and social harmony.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mental health, once considered peripheral, has emerged as a significant contributor to the burden of disease, affecting all age groups and demographics.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: From our youths grappling with stress and anxiety to adults and the elderly facing conditions like depression and schizophrenia, these challenges are societal concerns requiring collective action.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The GPC's passion for promoting mental well-being stems from a deep conviction that every individual deserves the opportunity to live a fulfilling life, unencumbered by the shadows of mental health issues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In our numerous engagements with constituents, mental health professionals and advocates, educators and students, workers and retirees, young and old, the recurring theme is clear – mental health is everyone's business.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But business as usual for mental health issues will not do.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With the escalation of mental health issues globally, Singapore is not immune.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The 2022 National Population Health Survey revealed a concerning rise in mental health issues among Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This upward trend was also observed in the older age groups.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This House must recognise the multifaceted nature of mental health as a critical issue that transcends health, influencing our society and economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, we need a robust mental health ecosystem that is proactive in promoting mental well-being, not just reactive in addressing illness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Health GPC aims to refine this strategy constructively, aligning with global best practices while tailoring solutions to our unique societal context.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The National Mental Health Blueprint, initiated over a decade ago, marked a significant step in our commitment to mental health, emphasising early intervention and community support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Following this, the Community Mental Health Masterplan further expanded our reach, bringing mental health services closer to the community and underscoring the importance of a more inclusive approach.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This brings us to the latest newly introduced strategy, which builds upon the successes and learnings of the past, further emphasising the whole-of-society participation while introducing comprehensive and innovative approaches to address current challenges such as digital well-being, workplace mental health and the mental health of our youths.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But how does this strategy compare with other countries?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Countries like Australia, Canada and the UK have also developed comprehensive mental health strategies.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Canada takes on an indigenous-centred approach and the UK adopts a tiered approach.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore combines these insights with specific strategies suited to its diverse population.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our strategy emphasises preventive care and integrates mental health services into the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the product of the hard work of many agencies, mental health advocates and volunteer organisations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not just a medical concern, but it also significantly impacts our social fabric and economic stability.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mental health issues have a profound impact on our social ecosystem too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They influence the dynamics of interpersonal relationships and can be a source of considerable stress, leading to burnout and social isolation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When an individual struggles with mental health issues, those around them and their loved ones often bear a significant emotional and physical burden.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, I recently shared with the media a phase when my wife went through post-natal depression.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It was slightly prolonged, and it was not easy for me to see to my better half struggling; so too were the kids.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It was difficult for me to see my kids having to put a strong front in front of their mother.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I was often worried how it might affect them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In workplaces, an employee's untreated depression can lead to decreased productivity and morale, impacting team dynamics and overall organisational health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within our communities, the social isolation experienced by those with mental health issues can diminish the sense of belonging and support, which is a vital core for a cohesive society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A robust ecosystem is not just about treating mental illness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also about fostering overall mental well-being at every level of the society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some time back, I encountered a youth struggling silently with anxiety.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sara, not her real name, is a bright student, but her performance started to decline.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Then, she missed classes, sometimes with medical leave, sometimes without.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: She struggled to submit her assignments and soon, isolated himself.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recognising the signs, her peers and I reached out.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And after many, many tries, she agreed to meet the school counsellor who, after a long period, eventually referred her to the Institute of Mental Health (IMH).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This intervention marked a turning point for her, and she gradually learned to manage her anxiety.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Sara's struggle, her journey of silence, is difficult.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But she received the support she needed and that underscores the importance of early intervention and comprehensive mental healthcare.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Her experience not only highlights the challenges faced by individuals grappling with mental health issues but also illuminates the path through which they can find hope and healing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we pivot to examining the strategic shifts in mental health support, Sara's story serves as a poignant reminder of why these shifts are necessary.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The three strategic shifts, in tandem, will allow the strategy to not only catch individuals like Sara earlier in their journey but also ensure that every step towards recovery is supported by a cohesive network of care and understanding.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am grateful for the invaluable insights gained, bringing forth a spectrum of concerns and suggestions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The lack of mental health professionals was also highlighted.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Within the education setting, through the Singapore Teachers' Union that I am a part of, there was also feedback for more para-educators and school counsellors to support the students and simultaneously lighten the load of teachers who may have find the administrative aspects of counselling quite a bit on their plate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe we can do more to support teachers in doing what they do best: caring for, planning and executing the best lessons for their students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The issue of parental consent for minors seeking mental health services has emerged as a significant barrier too, especially when parents might not fully grasp the critical nature of mental health support or may be hesitant to seek help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our concerns related to the strategies is as follows – the role and functions of the Mental Health Office, with many debating which Ministry it should be positioned under.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I do believe that the current set-up is appropriate, but we should empower them in two areas.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Office can co-create a comprehensive scenario guide with stakeholders.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could the Office look into and ensure the quality of these programmes and certify the volunteers and professionals within?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I firmly believe that today's debate should not simply be about putting up a laundry list.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about putting forth sensible suggestions to address concerns.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As I penned my suggestions, I ended up with an acronym, similar into my first Adjournment Motion in 2020.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And although I promised it would be the last, the acronym remains relevant in today's Motion, albeit with slight tweaks.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mental health literacy is about recognising that it is okay to reach out.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about seeing a friend's withdrawal not as coldness but as a cry for help and feeling confident to offer a hand.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about parents understanding their child's silence is not just a phase.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I envision mental health literacy as a catalyst, a catalyst that unites us, fostering empathy and guiding us in how to be there for each other in times of need.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To that end, mental health literacy must be viewed not only as knowledge about mental disorders and their risk factors but also as a construct that promotes positive mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, mental health literacy cannot be limited to children, adolescents and young adults only.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our efforts must be made to extend literacy programmes to adults and the elderly too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But, like any other toolbox, it cannot be more than a mere collection of resources.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It needs to be an integrated part of everyday life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It cannot also be just another "first aid box" – you bring it out in moments of crisis.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, this toolbox should be complemented with workshops and interactive sessions, showing parents not only how to use these tools but also how to approach their children with empathy and support, ensuring that the toolbox becomes a bridge to stronger family connections.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My suggestion is to work with existing networks like the Ministry of Education's (MOE) COMmunity and Parents in Support of Schools (COMPASS), which can amplify efforts, leveraging their engagement with the school-home-community triangle.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond formal education settings, there is a need for varied and engaging programmes to complement mental health literacy efforts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In October last year, M3@Jalan Besar and the Health Promotion Board (HPB) conducted a Mental Wellness programme named "Cinta Minda", loosely translated as "loving your mind".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Participants were engaged in an interactive theatre performance and critique a short film.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What happened was a lively sparkling discussion on approaches to mental health challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Tailoring these educational efforts to suit diverse community needs and cultural contexts is key to complement mental health literacy efforts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we move towards a more community-based approach, we should explore expanding and nurturing t e number of access points, specifically, in shared safe spaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It can be gardening, sports, or the arts, which can significantly affect our mental well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Last year, I attended "Prompting Feelings," an innovative artificial intelligence (AI)-powered art exhibition, a collaboration between the Singapore Association for Mental Health (SAMH) and R/GA, a creative agency.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It featured eight artists sharing their journeys with mental health disorders through AI-generated artworks, bending technology with human emotions to provoke conversations and understanding around mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Most recently, I visited Thought Partner Studio, a vibrant example of how art can be a therapeutic medium, bringing people together in co-working spaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such initiatives highlight the importance of accessible, shared environments where communal activities based on shared interests can contribute positively to mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are catalysts where connections deepen, understanding blossoms and support networks flourish, where everyone find sense of belonging.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am grateful that the strategy emphasises screening, especially for expecting mothers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To that end, I reiterate the need to treat mental health screenings just as how we would treat physical health screenings.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Similar to how physical screenings identify health issues and guide targeted interventions, mental health screenings can also offer insights into our mental well-being, paving the way for informed steps towards improvement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I remember over a year ago, when my doctor advised me to lose some weight and get more active, I went all out to achieve the desired health targets.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I came back to him 13 kilogrammes lighter and he was a bit too shocked.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This can be similarly replicated for mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If I know that my happiness index is low – by the way, there is no such thing as a happiness index – I will try my best, so that by the next screening when I see my doctor, that number will improve.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Just like our physical health, we will make strides to ensure that our mental health is well looked after.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Enhancing our approach to mental health begins with early and accessible screenings, integrating them into the educational and workplace environments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my previous speeches, I emphasised the critical importance of mental health breaks, or "time-outs".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These are essential in managing stress and preventing burnout.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I mentioned burnout extensively in my maiden speech.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Most recently, Liverpool Football Club manager, Jurgen Klopp, cited being burnt out and opted to take a break and everyone, opposition teams especially, embraced it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It shows that people know what burnout means.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Creating a culture where it is acceptable to take a moment for mental well-being can make a significant difference in the schools and workplaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about recognising and respecting our mental health needs as much as our physical health needs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If I can use Sara’s example again as a context, she can take a mental health time-out anytime during the semester.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a way to encourage students like Sara to acknowledge their struggles without fear of judgement, ensuring that they are not alone.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This blend of empowerment and care creates an environment where students or workers feel seen and supported, fostering a culture of understanding and early intervention.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The final "S" refers to spiritual health, another component of the seven health dimensions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about cultivating inner peace and a sense of purpose, values and connection, regardless of one's faith and belief system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In nurturing this dimension, we embrace practices that foster a sense of meaning and resilience, crucial aspects of self-coping mechanisms in our holistic approach to mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Spiritual health is not to be conflated with religious faith, even if it could encompass it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Spiritual health emerged in many conversations with the community, especially the Indian and Malay/Muslim communities and engagement sessions with the young people too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Just two weeks ago, at a young PAP annual mental health dialogue, a young lady shared her five "F"s for good mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Family, Friends, Fitness, which is also health, Finances and Faith.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Faith has shown to be a strong societal pillar and we have seen this during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Singaporeans drew strength from their diverse faiths and demonstrated remarkable unity and compassion, embodying the universal principle of neighbourly care found across religions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given the intertwined nature of community and religious life in Singapore, religious organisations have a unique opportunity to serve as platforms to advance our mental health efforts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By doing so, they can offer support, foster understanding and promote well-being within their communities, further illustrating faith's positive role in societal health and resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The perception that spirituality is the only solution to mental health issues was often highlighted.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, some people feel that individuals who suffer from mental health issues are actually being possessed by spirits and need religious intervention to get better.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This can give rise to stigma and fear in the community, causing individuals who need professional help to instead face stress and isolation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I recognise that in order to understand and treat mental health issues effectively, we do not need to separate spiritual issues from medical and professional therapy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We should also focus on raising awareness about mental health because it is our responsibility to eradicate any stigma associated with mental health issues and provide appropriate support for individuals who need help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is my hope that we can build a more caring society that is prepared to help individuals who suffer from mental health issues without judging them. : Mr Speaker, in lieu of this being a Mental Health Motion, I took note of the time and made sure that I kept my speech short.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I also want to give our many Members the chance to share their concerns from the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Before I conclude, I would like to take this opportunity to thank those who have engaged us and supported our efforts in mental health within the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For me, it was Dr Jonathan Kuek and Total Wellness Initiative as well as Sabrina Ooi and Calm Collective, who form part of the Jalan Besar Mental Wellness Network.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Likewise, organisations like Samaritans of Singapore (SOS), Singapore Association for Mental Health, Mental Act, Mental Health Film Festival, Club Heal, PERGAS and Silver Ribbon Singapore share the same passion and aspirations for advancing mental health in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many others and I apologise if I missed them out.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to emphasise our collective responsibility in advancing mental health in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This journey is not for the Government alone but for every segment of our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our schools and Institutes of Higher Learning are crucial in nurturing a supportive environment for our youth, integrating mental health literacy into their curriculum and providing adequate counselling resources.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers and workplaces must create cultures where mental health is prioritised and where employees feel safe to discuss their mental and well-being, and seek necessary support.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Community organisations, including religious groups, have the unique capacity to offer support networks and foster a sense of belonging and purpose, which is crucial for our nation's mental resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Every individual must be empowered and encouraged to take charge of their mental health, seek help when needed and support those around them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we move forward with this strategy, remember, no strategy is perfect.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What is important is that we remain committed to refining our approach, ensuring it remains relevant and practical.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In a recent dialogue session, I was asked about my aspirations for mental health in Singapore, and my answer is simple – it is about nurturing a resilient community that cares for one another, where anyone who needs help is able to get it without stigma and fear.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Together, let us build a nation where mental health is not just an aspiration, but a reality for all.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I look forward to the speeches from the rest.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You kept well within the time limit that you were given.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also note that many officeholders, including the Deputy Prime Minister, are slated to speak and this is attention long overdue.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, today I wish to focus my speech to call for a more holistic and well-rounded approach to mental health, which looks beyond lifting people out of situations of poor mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will speak on three broad areas: first, a call for a thriving and flourishing society to be built into policy formulation as an objective; second, for institutions and agencies to include and accurately promote good nutrition as part of our national mental health and well-being strategy; and third, for the promotion of structural barriers to mental health support and therapy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When we look at the larger picture, mental health is a fundamental part of our overall health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Globally, WHO has indicated that depression is one of the leading causes of disability and noted that people with severe mental health conditions die as much as two decades early due to preventable physical conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mental and social well-being does not mean just the absence or suppression of depression psychosis or any other mental health condition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What we need to consider, as part of today's debate on mental health, is to look beyond decreasing rates of mental ill-health and to discuss how to elevate well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having a thriving society has to stem from a study of how we can facilitate human flourishing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is about, in the words of Liber Marskey, growing the seeds rather than removing the weeds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I do not mean this replaces the importance and hard work undertaken by psychologists, psychiatrists, therapists and other workers and volunteers in the mental health sector who spent so much of their life working to tackle challenges brought about by mental illness and neurodiversity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is, without doubt, that we are in a much better position today to understand, reliably diagnose and provide the necessary support, medication and treatment, for those suffering from various neuropsychiatric conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Workers' Party MPs have, previously, called on the Government to ensure those in the mental health sector are supported in their work, for instance, by providing sufficient staffing and by facilitating financial support for those seeking the qualifications to become a counsellor.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That said, we should not rely solely on the disease model that has dominated psychology since the second world war.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead of asking, solely, how can we make miserable people less miserable, I would like us to also ask, "What is right with you?" Research in the last two decades has given us a better understanding of how we can measure and apply concepts of engagement, meaning and accomplishments in achieving well-being for individuals, organisations and societies, and that these areas are clear means by which we can improve well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In short, how can we go from ill-mental health to promote maximum flourishing?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not just about positive thinking or even toxic positivity but, instead, it is about figuring out how we can support our citizens in their journey to become the best versions of themselves.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The research shows that understanding and ultimately playing to our strengths, has the added advantage of helping us face adversity in a way that does not breakdown our well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is why we end up finding that people can still thrive in conditions of severe deprivation or conflict.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to entrench ideas of harnessing our strengths as individuals and as a society and use our own unique strengths as a solid foundation to build our future path forward.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can start this by helping our people understand what their own strengths are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The strengths-based approach is already being undertaken in the social work sphere, and I believe that the experience the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) has here could inform more opportunities for Government agencies and institutions to be able to apply this approach to other areas of policy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As policymakers and political leaders, we should not look to the lowest common denominator and perpetuate an environment, which takes away the factors that people need to flourish.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from strengths, meaning, accomplishment and gratitude, another area which promotes well-being, is to identify an up-to-date common set of values as a nation which we embody.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To support this expanded approach to mental health, we should consider findings from existing longitudinal research on well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The authors also note that Singaporeans have, and I quote, "...become less happy, enjoyed life less and, have felt a decreased sense of achievement.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also felt that they did not have control over their lives and a sense of purpose." An interesting observation from this research is also the positive correlation between Singaporeans' satisfaction, with five out of six recognised democratic rights, and their overall satisfaction with life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The findings further indicated a decline in satisfaction of democratic rights across the years in 2011, 2016 and 2022.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The authors also note that more in-depth research is required to determine specific concerns and to implement initiatives to better engage the citizenry and, I believe, that this is worth looking further into.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Presently, there are also ongoing studies that dwell into the allocation of financial resources within Singaporean families toward the families' well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These findings will be instructive, particularly in an environment marked by stresses associated with resource scarcity, in the wake of cost-of-living and climate-related concerns.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such studies may also prove to be pivotal in shaping our national policies spanning, economic, housing, health and social domains, all of which are aimed at fostering a holistic advancement of overall well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can leverage such findings to set the trajectory of our policies to better support Singaporean families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The research initiatives I mentioned above also dovetail nicely with WHO recommendations to ensure that high-quality research and data are available to specific societies and populations, so that we better understand the driving factors that enable Singaporean families to flourish.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also have to consider high-quality research in areas such as positive physical health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Studies in the US and Europe have found that patients with more optimism suffer from statistically significant lower rates of cardiovascular disease and decreased mortality rates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the effects are comparatively smaller for other diseases such as infectious illness and cancer, they remain noteworthy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the moment, I am not aware of similar research being done in Singapore to explore the potential correlation between traits such as optimism and improved physical health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If the findings are replicated here, this would further reinforce the call to delve deeper into understanding how to enable our citizens to flourish beyond just being free from physical and mental health pathologies, but also to flourish in all aspects of their well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, no discussion about enhancing and protecting mental health in a holistic manner can be done without mentioning our diet and lifestyle.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The emerging field of research about the effect that our everyday diet has on our well-being and mood is one that has much to offer.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Conversely, it has also been found that a diet that is high in refined sugars correlates to impaired brain function.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would be a shame if we do not seriously consider the scientific evidence surrounding foods that support good mental health and implement policies that make it easier to ensure that our diets complement and support our brains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The field of nutritional psychiatry is an emerging one.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, I hope that we can use our education and public health systems to include ways in which we can facilitate incorporating eating for a healthy brain into our everyday life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means eating more varieties of vegetables, fruits and less processed foods, as well as ensuring that we have adequate intake of healthy fats and fibre, all of which also promote good physical health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can begin by intensifying efforts to amplify and update existing healthy eating initiatives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The existing Healthy Dining Programme should emphasise clearly that healthy eating goes far beyond just merely counting calories.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from eating to reduce chronic illnesses such as diabetes and cardiovascular diseases, it should also consider the importance of consuming a variety of food types to promote maximal healthy brain function.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As the affordability of healthier food options remains a barrier to achieving healthy dietary practices, we must increase accessibility to healthier and more nutritious foods to as wide a segment of the population as possible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a fast-paced society with escalating concerns about the ever-rising costs of living, the prospect of incorporating whole foods, often more expensive than readily available highly processed options, adds another layer of concern.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With a global surge in food prices, it is the lower-income groups with the least resources that would face greater barriers to healthier food options.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The costs – both financial and also time costs – associated with eating healthily have to be mitigated further, to ensure that the ability to eat for a healthy brain is not one which is exclusive to those with greater economic means.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One way to achieve affordability and accessibility of healthier food choices is to ensure that our Government policies really lean into supporting the promotion of healthy diets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, in our drive to reach "30 by 30" for food sufficiency, we need to ensure that the bulk of the home-produced food would meet nutritional criteria.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The WHO has indicated that countries can stimulate the supply of nutritious food by creating large-scale predictable demand and making production and procurement of such foods more economically viable, and I believe that changes to our policies can be made to accommodate these aims.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Other areas which are promising and should be given more attention include supporting research which is specific to our geography and population, especially as it appears that we do have unique biological responses to certain foods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I spoke during last year’s Committee of Supply (COS) about the work being done by local enterprise, AMILI, to better understand the gut microbiome in local populations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given the gut-brain axis links the emotional and cognitive centres of the brain with peripheral intestinal functions, we should continue to pursue research in this area to better understand our own population’s needs and which foods would best support mental health and well-being, and to harness newer technologies such as artificial intelligence to bring down the costs associated with tailoring healthy food choices to specific sub-groups in the population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Employers, too, in their drive to support employee well-being, should consider ways in which to encourage healthy and mindful eating.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Small initiatives such as offering fruit and nut instead of sugary snacks and biscuits in the office pantry, providing more accessible storage and food preparation areas, providing access to water in more places and having regular healthy eating weeks or events to help employees understand how to incorporate eating for a healthy mind and body into their daily lives can go a long way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, to further enhance mental health support and break down the social stigma, we can do more to continue removing barriers to mental health support and therapy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will go a long way in ensuring that no one gets left behind.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The current lack of regulation of mental health workers is another area which warrants more attention.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is undoubtedly the case that there are many dedicated and committed workers in the mental health space that are doing amazing work in raising the well-being of our society, we have to move beyond providing guidance on professional and ethical conduct for psychologists, counsellors and therapists.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Setting up a regulating body with input from bodies, such as the Singapore Association for Counselling and Singapore Psychological Society, will ensure a universal standard of care and quality of care in the provision of such services to support mental health, and to ensure that there is at least a baseline level of training, expertise and ethical practice that underline the provision of such services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would not be a big step to use our 3Ms framework to better improve access to mental health treatments and interventions, as MediSave is already being approved for use for mental health services at places like IMH and polyclinics.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To close, although we have experienced headwinds in recent years and are rightly focusing on how to support increasing incidences of poor mental health, it would be remiss of us to not look more holistically at how to increase well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have to build on research about how positive interventions at the personal, community and policy level can have a protective factor through challenging times, and also to look at how our nutrition can better support us in our quest for good mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All of us have a role to play in working to improve our own well-being, and given that happiness spreads more easily than depression, the hope is that increased well-being can continue to ripple and spread to the wider community, so as to increase flourishing for all.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I stand in support of the Motion in the name of Dr Wan Rizal, my Parliamentary colleague.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, I will speak on insurance and, in particular, I direct my questions to the Ministers-in-charge of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) as well as the Minister for Health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the entire report, the word "insurance" appears just once in a footnote on page 28.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yet, insurance today is an integral part of the healthcare landscape.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It helps pool risk and safeguard Singaporeans from catastrophic bills arising from catastrophic unexpected illness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the public healthcare system, we have MediShield Life under the Ministry of Health (MOH).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But in addition to MediShield Life, many Singaporeans purchase health insurance from the private sector too – Integrated Shield Plans, critical illness cover, life insurance and other forms of general insurance – hoping to attain peace of mind and support for their families should the unforeseen or unimaginable happen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, it is a serious matter when a fellow Singaporean is worried about being denied insurance coverage or worried about being at the receiving end of an unreasonable or disproportionate decision by their insurer.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She could not get coverage for hospitalisation or critical illness, not even for non-pre-existing conditions unrelated to mental health.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have young Clementi residents who follow these issues and are concerned as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some are going through a tough time and want to seek help.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But sometimes these young Clementi friends also asked themselves, "What if they are subsequently labelled with a mental health diagnosis and thereafter cannot get insurance from a commercial insurance company?" Even if the actual number is not large, the effect, the sense of fear and anxiety about whether one might someday be denied insurance upon being labelled with the diagnoses, that fear extends beyond the number of persons who are actually affected and denied coverage.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, I put it to the Government and I put it to the Ministers, that all the efforts in the plan, all the efforts to increase subsidy for mental health care, in the mental health care ecosystem, all the efforts to improve access at multiple levels in the community and through various intermediaries, all the efforts to make workplaces more inclusive and more fair to persons with mental health conditions, I put it to the Government that we risk these policies and proposals not coming to their full potential or possibly even being undermined, as long as this issue of the private insurance market is not addressed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I raised broader issues of insurance coverage 11 years ago, in 2013, in an op-ed piece in The Straits Times.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I would just like to revisit some of what I said.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I said 11 years ago, in a well-functioning market of insurance providers and potential clients, an efficient outcome would be for the applicant's additional risk to be appropriately priced in through a higher premium.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But what we see instead is, even if someone has that additional risk from the pre-existing condition, the insurance company, more often than not, according to my residents, regards them as someone they would not want to insure at all.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Yes, indeed, there is MediShield Life in our public care system but, as the Minister for Health pointed out yesterday in response to my PQ on the private healthcare sector, the Minister for Health himself has acknowledged there is an important role for private healthcare ecosystems and that presumably includes the role of commercial insurance in the private sector in addition to the MediShield Life framework.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also mentioned previously that with modern computational methods – 21st century mathematics, in short; it is not completely rocket science – it should not be too difficult for insurers to estimate and calculate the right price for the additional risk.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But, again, we see perverse outcomes, and I think many Members in this House will have observed this with your own residents where that incremental increase in risk leads to a total denial of insurability from that insurance firm.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: While insurance in general is a business, the commercial health insurance market can and should serve a public good.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is heartening that the Government has published a National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy, outlining comprehensive moves to tackle this challenge from multiple angles.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the measures proposed in the paper and would like to make a few additional suggestions and seek some clarifications.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mental health disorders have been rising over the years to become one of the most common illnesses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Has there been a study to examine what are the possible causes or the common risk factors?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If causal effects cannot be determined, can we identify the risk factors that are common in many of the mental health cases?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, do many of the patients come from dysfunctional families or perhaps parents with a history of mental health issues?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the cases correlated to socioeconomic status or poor performance in work or school?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do patients have a supportive environment in terms of family members, friends, teachers, bosses or colleagues?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we are able to identify the highest risk factors, it can guide us on where we should focus our efforts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If such a study has been done, can MOH share the results?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is critical that we improve our capacity to care for, treat and support women going through pre- and post-natal depression and anxiety as we make efforts to increase our birth rate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOH update us on how effective this measure has been and whether there are plans to expand this to all hospitals and clinics including private ones?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In hospitals, patients' historical medical records are at the fingertips of the doctors in charge as these contain critical information for medical decisions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For patients with mental health disorders, are their mental health conditions and history also similarly available to the doctors?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Often, doctors need to brief patients on the possible side effects of certain treatments or the risks of surgery or present difficult choices for the patient to make.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Patients with mental health issues may not be able to handle such information or choices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If doctors have access to mental health information as well it can help them better know how to handle communication with the patients.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This underscores the urgency of prioritising the mental well-being of our students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Parliamentary Sitting on 27 July 2021, after this tragic incident, I urged the Minister for Education to consider implementing measures to monitor our students' mental well-being regularly and systematically, similar to the way we monitor their academic achievements and physical fitness every year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I would like to reiterate this call.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can be in the form of questionnaires that measure stress level, anxiety and depression.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similar tools have also been developed in MindSG and Mindline, which allow users to do self-assessments on their own stress levels and mental health risks.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These tools, however, rely on the users themselves taking the initiative.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The students who most need help may not take this initiative.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Conducting a mental health assessment each year using developed tools will help us identify students who need help and proactively reach out to them so that we can prevent such a tragic incident from happening again.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his Ministerial Statement, the Minister stated that the Ministry of Education (MOE) will strengthen the support network in our schools and ensure that all teachers will receive enhanced professional development on mental health literacy as a baseline.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Could I ask how many teacher-counsellors are deployed in schools as of today and what is the counsellor-student ratio?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What percentage of schools have two or more school counsellors?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do larger schools have enough counsellors to serve the entire school population?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are crucial metrics that define the effectiveness of mental health support in our educational institutions and should be tracked as part of our national mental health strategy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Specifically for the students and teachers of River Valley High School who were involved in the tragic incident, I would like to ask the Minister what support had been provided to them over the past few years to monitor their mental well-being and assist them in getting over the incident?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are they still coping well within our education system or has anyone fallen out of the system?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How many teacher-counsellors are deployed in River Valley High School today?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my conversations with people with mental health conditions, one of the biggest concerns is jobs – finding a job and keeping it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both job seekers and employees have reported an increase in discrimination due to mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government consider some form of wage subsidy for employers who recruit staff with mental health conditions, similar to the way we used subsidies to encourage employers to employ older workers in the past?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hopefully, such a subsidy can compensate for the discrimination.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we were going through very tough times together during the COVID-19 pandemic, we saw many acts of kindness towards one another in the community.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People gave out free masks, opened their homes to Malaysian workers who were stranded in Singapore after the Movement Control Order shut down the Causeway and made special efforts to support food and beverage (F&B) businesses that were suffering.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A few weeks ago, my father had a stroke when he was out alone.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He was unable to use his handphone to contact us.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fortunately, a student, who was nearby, came to his assistance.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She contacted our family and shared her location with me.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With that location, I was able to inform the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) and the ambulance reached the scene in 10 minutes!

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To the SCDF officers involved, I wish to thank you for being so excellent at your job.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The student continued to stay with my father until the ambulance came, which is a great comfort to us when we could not be there.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Her kindness is much appreciated by my family.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am grateful for all the people who shine like silver when the clouds are dark.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that as memories of the pandemic recede, we will not forget to continue to be gracious, kind and empathetic to the people around us, especially those who may be facing difficulties in their lives.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will go a long way towards improving the collective mental health of our society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Recently, a teenager who killed a student from River Valley High School was sentenced to 16 years in prison.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I once again urged the Minister of Education to regularly monitor the mental health of students, just as we monitor their academic performance and physical health every year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help us proactively reach out to students in need and prevent such tragedies from happening again.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my conversations with individuals suffering from mental illness, I have found that employment is one of their biggest concerns.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In recent years, there have been signs of increasing discrimination against individuals with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the pandemic, we have seen many acts of kindness.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People gave out masks for free, opened their homes to Malaysian workers stranded in Singapore and made special efforts to support the struggling F&B industry.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A few weeks ago, my father had a stroke while he was out alone.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He was unable to use his phone to contact us.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fortunately, he received help from a nearby female student.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She contacted our family and shared her location with me, allowing me to inform the SCDF.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ambulance arrived at the scene within 10 minutes!

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to express my gratitude to the SCDF for their excellent response.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the student continued to accompany my father until the ambulance arrived.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope that even as the pandemic gradually becomes a thing of the past, we will continue to show kindness and compassion to those around us, especially those facing difficulties in life.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will help to improve the collective mental health of our society. : Mr Speaker, the Progress Singapore Party supports the Motion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our collective commitment to the mental well-being of our citizens will define us as a compassionate and progressive society.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am glad that your father is well now.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Speaker, Sir, mental health is a globally complex issue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It often remains unseen and hidden beneath societal stigmas, especially in the context of Singapore and Asian cultures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A specific challenge lies in individuals' struggles to seek help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the report rightly identifies the need for more accessible services, I want to draw attention to a demographic needing specific focus – the mental well-being of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singapore is moving towards a super-aged society, with smaller family sizes becoming the norm.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our high-stress, high-cost living environment sets the stage for concerns like social isolation, loneliness and dementia among our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This highlights the urgency of prioritising mental health support for seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This seemingly small percentage translates to thousands of individuals silently battling mental health challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The question is this: are we equipped, as a society, to handle these challenges?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While MOH and the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) have made strides, there are areas for enhancement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, we need a more targeted approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The senior populace is diverse; individuals in their 60s differ significantly from those in their 70s and 80s.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our seniors are not of the same shade.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Engaging seniors effectively requires recognising differences in education, independence, employment status and technological acumen.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I vividly remember challenges when I was leading the Silver Generation Office, particularly engaging Merdeka Generation seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Through perseverance, we succeeded in rallying these seniors, fostering a connection rooted in mutual understanding of shared trials and tribulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our outreach must reflect diverse profiles by tailoring interventions and support to each cohort's needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A growing adversity is the lack of a comprehensive understanding of the evolving cohort of older adults.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moving forward, we must categorise our seniors into segments for effective interventions, including the well and active, the potentially at-risk and inactive, those frail and inactive due to physical or having mental health issues, individuals living independently, digitally adept and with fewer familial support systems, seniors who are financially stable and seniors from the lower socioeconomic group.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Leveraging the strengths and ambitions of different cohorts is critical, especially among the professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also shift the societal mental model from viewing elders as a burden to valuing their contributions and reframing their silver years as a different phase of life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A re-evaluation of our workforce's HR systems is paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By allowing older individuals to choose to continue working, we not only address manpower shortages but also provide them with a profound sense of purpose and financial independence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I commend the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM) consideration to legislate against workplace discrimination and address ageism.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is an important step towards extending retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The synergy between keeping our seniors meaningfully engaged in the workforce and enhancing their mental well-being is undeniable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is an endeavour that not only benefits that individual but also contributes significantly to the fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, we need a greater focus on building social networks for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Loneliness and the lack of social interaction are major risk factors for mental health issues in seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beneath the surface of seemingly ordinary lives, unseen ebbs and tides of depression and anxiety can sometimes pull our seniors under.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Studies consistently underscore the pivotal role that social connections play in fostering longevity and overall well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Encouraging informal networks to flourish can provide invaluable opportunities for socialisation among our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Healthier SG initiative and the emphasis on social prescriptions align with promoting well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should champion more grassroots initiatives and urge organisations, like the Housing and Development Board (HDB) and National Parks Board (NParks), to create more physical spaces conducive for these communities to congregate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Age-friendly environments with green spaces, accessible walkways and safe communal areas become vital.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These initiatives encourage seniors to venture beyond their homes, fostering social awareness, exercise and a sense of safety and comfort.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As part of a joint project by AIC, Singapore University of Technology and Design and the Centre for Liveable Cities, we conducted evidence-based research on the relationship between persons living with dementia, their caregivers and the built environment in Singapore's predominantly high-rise and high-density urban context.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must continue empowering seniors through digital tools and technology.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Limited access to mental health services, especially for those with mobility issues, can be a barrier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Expanding telehealth options and making services more readily available in eldercare facilities can bridge this gap.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the Government's efforts to assist seniors in embracing technology are commendable, harnessing technology to create interest groups and leverage existing digital social networks is imperative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An exemplary initiative is the use of platforms like Vintage Radio, catering to individuals aged 60 and above.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This platform serves as a conduit to disseminate information on critical health issues, such as sarcopenia.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, it encourages the formation of local groups, fostering opportunities for gatherings centred around activities like tea sessions, exercise regimens or sessions discussing healthy lifestyle choices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, seniors with mental health concerns must have convenient and affordable access to quality mental health services.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The silent struggles with mental health are particularly stark for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From the gnawing isolation that fuels depression to the constant worry that fuels anxiety, these invisible burdens weigh heavily on their hearts and minds.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These conditions, often masquerading as loneliness or physical ailments, can impact their daily lives significantly, robbing them of any joy and fulfilment they deserve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Misconceptions about mental health often prevent seniors from seeking help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Raising awareness and normalising conversations about mental well-being is imperative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Currently, the lack of options for assistance is pressing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can gain insights form other developed countries with ageing populations by understanding the ratio of seniors to geriatric counsellors, caseloads and waiting times.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another important aspect is the proactive implementation of preventive measures against mental health issues among seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Identifying effective therapies and interventions to prevent the onset of mental health conditions is paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should assess the optimal age to begin initiatives aimed at supporting seniors' mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our strategy needs to evolve to meet the diverse needs of today's senior cohort, recognising differences between various age groups, particularly the baby boomer generation and the PMETs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Preparing them for life transitions involves leveraging their strengths and aspirations, fostering social activity through work or engagement in interest groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: WHO defines mental health as a state of well-being encompassing psychological, emotional and social aspects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must pivot our focus from solely discussing mental illness to adopting a holistic, person-centric approach, acknowledging the five key components: physical, emotional, intellectual, financial and social.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By prioritising mental healthcare, we can bolster productivity, enhance self-image and fortify relationships.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Maintaining positive mental health and treating any poor mental health conditions are critical to stabilising constructive behaviours, emotions and thoughts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must address isolation and loneliness through a holistic and person-centric approach.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Technology serves as a force multiplier in enhancing mental healthcare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The use of telehealth to deliver services and support demonstrates promise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Initiatives that leverage technology not only streamline access but also create opportunities for innovation in mental healthcare delivery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, it is pertinent to underscore the significance of accessible and affordable professional geriatric mental healthcare.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This vital resource extends much-needed support to seniors grappling with various mental health challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our Pioneer and Merdeka Generations have weathered storms and setbacks throughout their lives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They possess a wealth of experience, wisdom and strength that we should tap into.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By fostering a supportive environment, acknowledging their struggles and celebrating their victories, we can empower them to thrive, even amidst their mental health challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, I urge each of us, legislators, Government officials, healthcare professionals, family members and every resident, to play our part in creating a society that prioritises the mental well-being of our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us champion open conversations about mental health, break down the stigma and normalise seeking help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Support community initiatives, volunteer time, resources and expertise to build social connections and combat isolation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Advocate for accessible and affordable mental health services, ensure every senior has the resources they need to care for their mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Embrace and respect our seniors, recognise their contributions, value their wisdom and celebrate their resilience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is an investment in the future of our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By working together, we can build a brighter tomorrow where every senior in Singapore can age with dignity, purpose and hope.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Together, let us ensure that our Silver Generation shines not just because of their past contributions, but also because of the bright future we create for them today.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I hold a Visiting Consultant Psychiatrist appointment in a restructured hospital and I am the Honorary Secretary of the Singapore Psychiatric Association.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that the range and scope of what we will discuss today and put forth to the House will be wide ranging and impactful and it will inform the way we, as a country, see mental health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I am hopeful that this will lead to meaningful change in the way we view discourse over mental health and how it informs public policy from herein.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health and well-being are not just an issue that resides in the realm and domain of healthcare and, for that, I am grateful to the five hon Members of the House who had put forth this Motion for us to debate and consider.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, that the debate is happening highlights two things.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The first is that the issue of mental health and well-being permeates through and is relevant to all aspects of our individual lives whether it be in school, at work or at home.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is even before we venture into the realm of mental illness.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health and well-being features in how we socially interact with one another, impacts how we perform and fulfil our roles at work and has a very direct relationship to our physical health as well.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The second is that there is a now wider awareness, realisation and imperative at the national level in recognising the cost to our society if we do not act and leave things as they be.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This was based on survey data from 5,725 adults collected via an online panel between April and June in 2022, with the results made public in April 2023.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These costs tend to come from absenteeism, reduced productivity and direct medical care, including hospital visits and admissions.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: There is also increasing awareness of the longer-term costs relating to intermediate and long-term care services, as well as indirect medical costs on family members and caregivers.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Similar patterns, Mr Speaker, and cost trends relating to mental health are evident not only in Singapore but the world over, and the costs of ignoring mental health and well-being are staggering.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: To that end, that the Government has promulgated the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy paper published in October 2023 is much welcomed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It covers good breadth and, importantly, gives a frame and structure towards the national strategy in dealing with mental health and well-being.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine many hon Members speaking today will approach the Motion with a wider population-level concern relating to the strategy paper.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The scope of my contribution to this debate will consider the professional aspects of clinical delivery of mental health, particularly at tier 4 of the Tiered Care Model articulated in the said strategy paper.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Tier 4 services are of high intensity, delivered by psychiatrists, psychologists and other multidisciplinary mental healthcare professionals in hospital settings, both inpatient and outpatient, to support those with high mental health needs.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: These services comprise specialist-led psychiatric assessments, psychological and medical interventions, including acute and emergency services.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: As far as the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy paper goes, tier 4 is the sharp tip of the strategy that deals with the most acute, challenging and complex of psychiatric cases.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I note that the strategy paper states that tier 4 services largely reside in hospitals which have their own competency development plans for clinical staff and would not be covered by the National Mental Health Competency Training Framework.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is important to ensure that tier 4 services keep up and remain in tandem with the larger national need and demand for mental health services.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I say this, conscious that I am one such psychiatrist, but it is not out of self-absorption of my specialty that I say this.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I argue that the numbers speak for themselves when taken in relative comparison to the number of psychiatrists per population in other developed countries and the widening waiting times for psychiatric visits in Singapore over the years.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This was the number given by the Ministry of Health (MOH) in response to a Parliamentary Question (PQ) by former Nominated Member of Parliament (NMP) Assoc Prof Walter Theseira in January 2020, four years ago.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: However, when compared to other developed countries, according to WHO data from dated numbers between 2015 and 2017, I could not find any data which was a bit more recent.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Based on that data, Norway has 48 per 100,000, Switzerland has 43, New Zealand has 28, Australia has 13, Japan has 11 and the US has 10 per 100,000 population.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is in relative comparison to Singapore at 4.4.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The second point is also that the waiting time for patients over the years also indicates a widening of waiting times for psychiatric subsidised visits in our public hospitals.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: So, 27 days for all public hospitals in 2018 and 29 days for IMH in 2020.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: So, we see a leap of that from 27, 29 and then 45 days, as of the response last year.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: As I emphasised in my Adjournment Motion in October 2023, median times, while helpful for healthcare planning of resources, only reflect 50% of the patient experience, and there is another 50% of patients referred to a psychiatrist that is seen beyond 45 days.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: So, we have a data point for 95% within three months, which is about 90 days, as of 2022.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: For sure, Mr Speaker, the numbers of psychiatrists are not everything in the delivery of mental healthcare.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: However, if we were to be serious about wanting to ensure that we are adequately resourced with expertise in our midst, surely, we need to look hard at these numbers and recognise how much better we can and should be in our delivery of mental healthcare services, especially at the specialist level of care where our patients are most vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: A good critical mass of experts in the field further helps us develop deeper expertise in sub-specialty areas, such as community psychiatry, child and adolescent psychiatry, psychogeriatrics, addictions, forensic psychiatry and psychiatric rehabilitation, and in key emerging treatment modalities, such as neurostimulation services for our patients.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The same experts can also inform other aspects of community care and education in the other tiers of the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I posit that this is difficult and hardly possible because the same experts are stretched to meet the bursting demand for inpatient and outpatient care services.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
