text: My second point, Mr Speaker, is in relation to clinical services provided by clinical psychologists.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: As we finesse our mental health strategy towards improving care, the Government should consider the feasibility of a regulatory framework for clinical psychologists.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This would be especially important for those working in tier 4 and in clinical settings in the community.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Where clinical psychologists are concerned, there must be clarity over the prerequisite training and experience in clinical settings as they interface with patients regularly, patients who are vulnerable and are seeking care for their mental health needs.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: While psychologists' skillsets may be transferable to areas such as sports, education and organisations, the specific training for clinical psychologists needs to be further deliberated, structured and regulated in clinical settings, such as hospitals and outpatient clinics, and with the availability of adequate supervision.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Respectfully, there are many different branches of psychology, such sports psychology, education psychology and organisational psychology, but clinical psychology skillsets required in the delivery of mental healthcare and clinical services are, indeed, distinct and different.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: To register my point, Mr Speaker, there are 641 psychologists registered under the directory of psychologists maintained by the Singapore Psychological Society (SPS).

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It remains the case that MOH does have a regulatory framework for other allied health specialties, such as occupational therapists, physiotherapists and speech therapists, and we should allow for no less for clinical psychologists to give assurance to patients that the standards of care are high, commensurate with their needs and they can be assured of quality of care.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: From a healthcare manpower planning standpoint, accreditation and regulation would allow the Ministry sight of how many clinical psychologists the country and our public hospitals now have and need to ensure timely and accessible care as part of the wider National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: My third point relates to accessibility of tier 4 and its associated mental healthcare services and speaks to what I shared at the Adjournment Motion in October 2023.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government can and should do more to ensure tier 4 services continue to be accessible to Singaporeans, even as it seeks to buttress the overarching national strategy over the initial three tiers of care.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I note the Government intends to increase psychiatric beds by 2030, but it is also important that for mental healthcare, the capacity for inpatient beds, rehabilitation programmes, psychiatric nursing homes and outpatient clinics keeps in tandem with the anticipation in demand in the coming years.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, hon Member Mr Yip Hon Wing's speech earlier spoke to the varied and increasing complex mental healthcare needs in Singapore's ageing society now and in the foreseeable future.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The better our subsidy and financial support coverage for treatment options at tier 4, the more focused treatment approaches can be and with good outcomes for our patients.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of insurance coverage for accessibility to mental healthcare services, as passionately expressed and outlined by hon Member and fellow medical professional Dr Tan Wu Meng, I urge the Government to maintain sight of this developing space to ensure adequate, fair and equitable insurance coverage for all.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This is because under the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy, this patient would have already exhausted all the initial three tiers of care and there is urgency in the need for specialist assistance by this point.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It makes sense that this could be reduced if the expressed strategy were to achieve its full potential.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If the proximal three tiers are effective and adequately address mental health needs early, it would follow that at tier 4, there would be less referrals overall to our specialist services in hospitals and this, in turn, lends capacity to manage the care of higher intensity, specialist-led cases.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, if we set our mind to it and acknowledge that this is the outcome we wish to attain as part of our standard of care at tier 4 and that mental health and well-being are important as a priority for our nation, then we must galvanise the resources necessary to realise this vision.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the health issue, there is great impetus in the social and economic domains to be realised for Singapore in the medium to longer term.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my comments, I am in support of this Motion.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will focus my speech on the case for better support for mental wellness at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My speech will build upon parts of my Adjournment Motion on Strengthening Mental Wellness at the Workplace which I delivered last January in this House.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most adult Singaporeans spend most of their time at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, suffice to say that better support at the workplace will make a significant difference to the overall wellness of our society and create positive ripple effects for other segments in our community.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, greater mental health literacy acquired at the workplace can equip parents to support their children back home and empower neighbours to support one another in the community.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such findings are consistent with realities on the ground.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in the 2023 Health and Well-being Survey by the National University of Singapore’s (NUS) Office for Health and Well-being revealed that workplace mental health interventions can help to activate the building blocks for human flourishing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These building blocks were measured as positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning and accomplishments and health, PERMA + H, a model developed by Dr Seligman at the University of Pennsylvania.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The survey revealed that employees from departments who promote mental health are 2.53 times more likely to have a high PERMA score, compared to those who are not.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This demonstrates that investing in mental wellness directly benefits a firm's bottom line, aligning with strategic economic goals and sustainable business growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is to help every Singaporean thrive in the workplace and not just survive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is about helping every Singaporean to maximise their potential and derive purpose and meaning in their endeavours.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MOH’s Health and Well-being Strategy for 2023 acknowledges the increasing prevalence of mental health disorders and emphasises preventive care.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It proposes a tiered care model that focuses on supporting employers, customising care, reducing stigma, improving employment opportunities for individuals with mental health conditions, promoting re-integration and preventing discrimination.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I support these measures proposed to improve workplace mental health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I echo the call for more support to be rendered to employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a collective responsibility – while employers set the tone, every member of the organisation must contribute to systemic improvements in workplace mental health.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have five suggestions to enhance the support to employers further.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As it is often said: "You can’t improve what you don’t measure." Enhancing the effectiveness of existing measurement tools is crucial in improving mental wellness at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, tools like iWorkHealth and Human Capital Diagnostic Tool (HCDT) operate in silos, focusing on specific aspects of workplace well-being without interconnection. iWorkHealth is an online, self-administered psychosocial health assessment tool for companies and employees to identify common workplace stressors, while HCDT evaluates the broader organisational health and human capital aspects.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach limits the understanding of how individual and organisational factors interplay in workplace mental health.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To better support mental health at work, we should blend tools like iWorkHealth and HCDT. iWorkHealth looks closely at each person's mental health while HCDT checks the overall health of a company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By combining them, we can obtain a fuller picture – understanding both what each employee is going through and how the workplace might be affecting them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This way, companies can create better plans to help everyone, considering both individual needs and the work environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, we need to promote greater awareness and adoption of these measurement tools among employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Government if there are any specific plans in the pipeline to promote greater adoption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, scaling up Well-being Champions Networks to share best practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The recent launch of the online portal Kaleidoscope, as part of the newly minted Well-being Champions Network, is one such example of how various tools and resources can be consolidated into a single platform to promote more effective access to workplace mental health resources.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Using Kaleidoscope, members of the network can access physical and online networking events, workshops and training, an online forum to discuss issues with fellow members and expert personnel, tailored virtual consultations with professional consultants and a directory of curated articles, case studies and best practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And what are the plans to increase the membership numbers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would also like to clarify if the services offered through the network are accorded free of charge to members or what are the benefits for members beyond networking.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For reference, Hong Kong has established a Mental Health Workplace Charter under its Occupational Safety and Health Council Ordinance, which is a statutory board.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I wish to emphasise the dynamic nature of well-being, which varies along a spectrum, with individuals experiencing fluctuations over time.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Recognising this, the WellNUS Mental Health Framework plays a pivotal role in mapping out the various stages of an individual’s well-being journey, providing a systematic approach to identify necessary initiatives and key stakeholders for support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A framework serves as a blueprint for employers, especially our SMEs in supporting their employees across different stages – from maintaining well-being, through periods requiring intervention and support, to recovery and the critical transition back to work.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Crucially, this framework facilitates the smooth reintegration of employees into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It ensures that as they return, they do so to an environment that actively supports and nurtures their recovery.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Wider adoption of this framework can significantly enhance the support provided to employers and employees across various sectors, leading to a more inclusive and supportive workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is not merely a matter of policy but ensuring effective translation on the ground.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Establishing an organisational framework is a good first step but we must recognise that organisations engaging in different activities will have different work settings and stressors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, it is necessary to contextualise the framework based on industry and workplace nuances.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, contextualisation and customisation often limit the scalability of a framework.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, the next logical step is to contextualise the framework for organisations in similar trade and workplaces.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will better support TACs in customising the organisation framework for their members and adopting mental health tech solutions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Four, scaling up of HR professionals and Chief Human Resource Officer (CHRO)-as-a-service.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my Adjournment Motion speech last January in this House, I highlighted the potential of broadening the roles of Human Resource (HR) managers, or other relevant managers, to encompass workplace mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to empower HR managers to oversee well-being policies, programmes and strategies within organisations, a move that balances efficacy with financial prudence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Institute of Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) has been instrumental in this area.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, I hope that MOM can consider initiating collaborations between NUS and IHRP to infuse the organisation's mental health framework into existing HR frameworks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must also recognise the constraints faced by SMEs, which often operate with leaner teams and limited resources.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A similar model exists with the Chief Technology Officer (CTO)-as-a-Service programme by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) that enables SMEs to engage digital consultants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through a relevant organisation such as IHRP, MOM can consider offering CHRO-as-a-service and adopting the workflow as a possible tool to guide companies in improving mental wellness policies at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond HR professionals, we need every employee to play an active role in strengthening mental wellness at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I wish to reiterate my previous call to SkillsFuture, urging the introduction of new Continuing Education and Training (CET) courses, specifically in the realms of peer support and managerial support training.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we move forward, I propose that SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) updates its core critical skills courses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This update will enable employers to access a growing pool of individuals trained in implementing mental wellness policies and initiatives, a critical step in fostering a supportive work environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A key skill set that we should aim to cultivate across all levels of our workforce is psychological first aid.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: WHO defines psychological first aid as a method to support people in crisis, focusing on meeting basic needs, showing care and concern, and respecting their culture, dignity, and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This approach is akin to traditional physical first aid but focuses on mental health crises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Regarding the critical core skills training under SkillsFuture, there are already mentions of relational skills, soft skills, developing people and self-management but a notable lack of "psychological first aid".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By making psychological first aid training a more prominent and integral part of our skills development framework, we ensure that our workforce is not only professionally competent but also mentally resilient and supportive, creating a healthier, more compassionate workplace for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And five, recognising employers who implement mental wellness policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A critical aspect of promoting mental wellness at the workplace is recognising and incentivising employers who take proactive steps.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The annual National Workplace Safety and Health CARE, or Culture of Acceptance, Respect and Empathy, Award is a commendable initiative, spotlighting organisations that exemplify outstanding mental well-being practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These organisations are celebrated as model employers, setting a benchmark for others.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In our quest to create a more robust recognition system, partnerships are key.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre's (NVPC) Company of Good framework, which now includes mental wellness policies in its evaluation criteria, presents an excellent partnership opportunity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This consolidation not only streamlines the recognition process but also makes it easier for job seekers and consumers to identify exemplary employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, a unified approach can potentially draw more attention and resources, and reduce duplications and wastages, thus elevating the profile and impact of these awards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, implement a comprehensive tool for employers to measure workplace mental wellness considering individuals and organisational factors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, scale up best practices sharing opportunities for employers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Four, provide HR professionals, CHRO-as-a-service, and individual workers with mental health literacy to effectively implement frameworks and policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And five, consolidate recognitions, such as WSH Care awards and NVPC Company of Good, to facilitate the identification of exemplary employers, promoting a positive cycle of prioritising workplace mental wellness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Strengthening mental wellness at the workplace is a social mission worth advancing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us partner with our enterprises to make mental wellness a cornerstone of our national economic and social strategy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That way, every Singaporean can maximise their potential and derive purpose and meaning in their endeavours.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: She had been a part of our team since 2008 and was known for her quiet dedication and tireless work ethic.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Often staying late into the night, Mdm X was battling a private challenge unknown to us, a struggle with hoarding.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A tragic fire at her home, fuelled by the very items that once brought her comfort, ultimately led to her untimely death.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This event deeply affected both myself and our entire company, highlighting a stark reality.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Despite our close-knit interactions over 13 years, we were unaware of the mental health struggles Mdm X faced.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With the support from the company, these groups engage in informal outings and fitness activities, encouraging open dialogue and support, not just in physical health but in all aspects of life.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: They share photographs and positive affirmations, building a network of assistance and encouragement and creating a safe space for members to seek help and peer support.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This incident underscores the critical role businesses play in promoting mental health and well-being as part of a national effort.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This tool is invaluable and I wished our company would have had this tool earlier.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope the Government will continuously engage with businesses for feedback after the roll-out to continue improving on this tool.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, not all HR professionals have the necessary skillsets and experience to handle workplace mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will make the appointment of mental well-being champions more effective.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These include enhancing Government-Paid Paternity Leave (GPPL) and Government-Paid Maternity Leave (GPML), embracing the tripartite standard, obtaining Progressive Wage Mark accreditation, and now, supporting a forward-thinking workplace culture that emphasises the mental well-being of employees.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Implementing such a framework would significantly speed up our nation's efforts to forge a workforce that is both more inclusive and equitable.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: My third recommendation therefore continues to emphasise the importance of recognising companies that support these national-level initiatives and highlighting those that excel in these areas.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We should consider integrating this recognition framework with tangible economic incentives, such as prioritisation in Government procurement processes, already associated with Progressive Wage Mark accreditation and possibly, temporary enhancements to foreign workforce access.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such measures would serve as a strong motivation for businesses to align with these national objectives.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Another focus area covered in the paper is the customisation of mental health support for specific occupational needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Working with MHA and Ministry of Defence to strengthen mental health support for Police officers and National Servicemen is a good start.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But there is scope to expand this approach to other occupational groups, such as frontline services sectors that are susceptible to specific mental health stressors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As suggested by my hon colleague, Mr Edward Chia, my fourth recommendation is for the Government to support sectoral agencies and trade associations and chambers to work together to develop a holistic mental health support system for their sector.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I have spoken quite a bit on mental health and well-being, and this is an opportune moment to emphasise that workplace well-being is a multifaceted concept that cuts across physical health, emotional wellness, social connectivity, financial security and professional growth and fulfilment.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the foundation of holistic well-being is physical health.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As a fundamental baseline, companies must provide a stable environment for employees to work safely and without risks to health.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But the responsibility of a company goes beyond that.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore essential to encourage workplaces to promote physical activity, offer healthier meal options and facilitate regular health screening.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Emotional well-being, influenced by the workplace atmosphere, plays a pivotal role here.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Business leaders should take the lead in championing a respectful, collaborative and cohesive workplace setting where disputes can be resolved amicably, and a culture of inclusion and communication is celebrated.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must be intentional about defining and implementing work-life harmony strategies that balance operational and commercial demands alongside employees' need to recharge, spend time with loved ones and pursue personal passions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Companies should provide employees with structured opportunities for continuous learning, skills development and career advancement.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This balanced approach aims to foster an environment where empathy and endurance coexist, ensuring mental well-being is recognised and supported without diminishing the value of resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On a lighter note, to everyone celebrating Chinese Lunar New Year and facing a mental health issue from relatives, remember, a healthy dose of bak kwa and pineapple tarts will help.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I propose to take a healthy break now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and I will take the Chair at 4.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.25 pm until 4.45 pm.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Mental health must be a key priority for this House and this Government.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My speech today will focus on an area I am passionate about: the mental health and well-being of our children and youth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My speech takes into account the plans announced in the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy and considers how we can do even more for our children and youth.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We often talk about the potential of youth; about how they are our hopes and dreams, and how they will shape the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We tell them that the world is full of rainbows to follow and opportunities to seize.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But youth can also be a difficult time, with many transitions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Childhood is a time when we form the basis for our relationships and friendships, which greatly influence our future physical and mental health throughout our lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then you start school and, all too quickly, academic pressures build up, pressure to meet the expectations of teachers and principals, parents and, more often than not, our own.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Adolescence and young adulthood are thought to be particularly tumultuous times in neuro-psychological and physical development, when mental disorders typically emerge.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The second Singapore Mental Health Study, conducted in 2016, revealed a significant association between younger age and mental disorders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In particular, young adults aged 18 to 34 had the highest lifetime prevalence for any mental disorder.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In 2017, it was reported that mental illness was the largest contributor to years lost to disease among young people aged 10 to 34 in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fast forward a few years, the statistics tell us the problem has not only persisted, it is getting worse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not only are we seeing rising numbers, we are also seeing more severe and complex mental health needs amongst our children and young people, including among those with learning disorders and autism.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can identify determinants of health and their impact on mental health and well-being, which include social, economic, cultural, relational and physical environments, such as housing and diet.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some children and youths are still feeling the effects of isolation and uncertainties due to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some parents are dealing with their own mental health and well-being issues.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They are stressed, worried about their jobs, families, money problems, the rising costs of living, nevermind recognising their children’s needs and helping them to develop resilience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To help these children, we need to also help their parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To relieve the pressure that is building up and increasing the risk of a mental health tsunami where the system simply cannot cope any longer, we need to focus on prevention and on population health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If this sounds familiar, it is because we have come to this conclusion before when we launched Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And this brings me to a core tenet – if the disease burden of mental health is up there with more commonly understood diseases, mental health and how we deal with it must be on par with physical health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The principles of Healthier SG must equally apply and, indeed, mental health must be integrated in the Healthier SG framework.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is no Healthier SG without a mentally Healthier SG.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I welcome the shift envisioned in the National Strategy, moving from a focus on treatment and institutionalisation, to focus equally on prevention and early identification and intervention in the community, on building an effective mental health ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I welcome the plans to do more upstream, addressing societal driving forces, raising awareness and building mental resilience and coping abilities in our people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Specifically for youths, I would like the focus areas and interventions identified, including a post-discharge intermediate facility for youths at risk of suicide, scaling up mental health literacy efforts for children and youths starting from preschools, improving the support to parents and promoting safe use of the online space and digital mental health platforms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The first, A, is a young Woodlands resident.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She was in Primary 1 when the pandemic struck.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She developed a phobia of falling sick and dying.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She started to refuse to go to school or would cry in school until the teachers called her parents to pick her up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She developed chest and stomach pains that resulted in frequent trips to the doctors and the Accident and Emergency department.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But each time, the finding would be, "Everything is normal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We do not know what is wrong." This went on for more than a year until her mother asked for a referral to a psychologist.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She was then referred to her school counsellor.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While the school had failed to identify the early signs, once diagnosed, they gave A very good support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She had an anxiety toolkit of coping mechanisms.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Whenever she felt a panic attack attacking, she could leave class immediately and run to the counsellor’s office.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The counsellor would often sit with her at recess and talk to her.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She would not be scolded for being late for school.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her teacher sent her daily personal notes of encouragement.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She has joined a co-curricular activity (CCA) after school and has a close group of friends.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her parents credit the school’s accommodative and flexible approach as being key to helping her get better.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In contrast, the subject of my second story, B, did not get the same support from her school.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Now, in her earlier 20s, B had always been anxious about her academic performance, even though she did well.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the transition from her all-girls secondary school to a top junior college (JC) was a difficult one.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She was harassed by a group of boys.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They made comments about her, her looks and her body on social media.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The harassment spilled over into the physical world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She developed severe anxiety and it affected her grades, which made her anxious.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She was then referred to a psychiatrist and a psychologist at a restructured hospital, whom she still sees today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She eventually dropped out of JC to go to polytechnic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The people were nicer, the teachers kinder and more patient, but she still struggled.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then she went to university in Australia, where she experienced a very different culture, one where people were much more open about their mental health.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The university had tailored Disability Support Plans for students with physical or mental issues.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She estimated 30% of students were on some sort of support plan.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her colleagues and supervisors were open, understanding and supportive of one another’s mental health needs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: After another episode which forced her to leave her job for three months, she was surprised to be warmly welcomed back to work. "It was like they were really happy to see me back", she said.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In the community there were regular large-scale mental health carnivals to raise awareness and help people learn coping skills.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There would be specific organisations presenting to different audiences, for example, people from the military or parents who had lost a child to suicide.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Often, the speakers would have mental health conditions themselves or be caregivers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The specificity helped to make people feel that there were people who really understood what they were going through.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Now, back in Singapore and looking for a job, B feels a lot of uncertainty about her future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But her self-awareness and understanding of her condition helps.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her mother told me it had been a struggle to learn how to support her daughter and she is still learning.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He was a playful child who liked to play pranks on people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But at the tender age of 14, he was diagnosed with bipolar disorder after his first suicide attempt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He struggled, despite seeking treatment at the Child Guidance Clinic, despite the strong support of his mother, who was both his caregiver and the sole breadwinner for the family as C’s father also had bipolar disorder.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He refused to see a school counsellor or psychologist after the first session.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His condition deteriorated further when he entered National Service (NS) and turned 18, when he was transitioned from the Child Guidance Clinic to IMH.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He did not feel like he belonged with "all those crazy people" he would see in the waiting room.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He attempted suicide again and was discharged from NS.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He started working but found it difficult to hold down jobs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When he became unstable due to anxiety, employers considered him a risk and terminated his employment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He had no one to turn to at work who understood.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Despite all these struggles, C got married and he and his wife bought a Build-To-Order (BTO) flat and had a baby.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His wife was aware of his condition and supported him, making sure he took his medication, and his mother supported them financially.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But his mother-in-law started belittling him, calling him a "useless idiot" and accusing him of faking illness so he did not have to work, even after his mother went to see her to try and make her understand.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They accorded him little dignity and respect and even kept his baby from him.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Not long after, he took methamphetamine again, this time, a huge dose.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His wife then filed for divorce and moved her parents into their home.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His sister told his mother that his wife should just divorce him because of his bipolar condition, just like his mother had eventually divorced her own bipolar husband.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: His mother took him back to her house and took him to NAMS.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: After his discharge, he went back to NAMS and was told he was fine, to go home and just come back for counselling in 10 days.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He asked for his favourite food and started eating again, he talked about plans for the future.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But two days after coming back, in the evening, he went out for a walk.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He did not allow his mother to accompany him, insisting he was fine.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But a couple of hours later, his mother received his suicide note over WhatsApp.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It said he could not bear the cravings any longer and he did not want to be a burden to his family any longer.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It was his own brother who found him after a frantic search.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When I heard C’s story, I wept for C and for his mother who had lost her first-born son.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: She has a second son who suffers from depression, a bright boy in primary school whose life trajectory changed when he went to an elite boys' secondary school and found himself unable to keep up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These stories can be hard to listen to.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But they are real, and they point to the scale and complexity of the challenge, and this is why Dr Wan Rizal, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Edward Chia and I have filed this Motion and why so many Members are rising to speak.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The National Strategy on Mental Health and Well-being is a very important step.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I believe we can do even more, particularly in the difficult area of driving societal change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: No amount of Government interventions with new structures, new care models, new resources and new legislations will work if we do not, as a society, transform.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we do not, as a society, become more aware of what people around us are going through and make it safe for people to be more open about the mental health challenges that they or their loved ones face; if we do not accept that not everyone is able to deal with it no matter how much they try; if we do not become more understanding and compassionate; and if we do not stand together to act to improve the mental health and well-being of every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The National Strategy recognises the need to better equip parents to support their children’s mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It highlights strong relationships with their children as a foundation for strengthening children’s mental and emotional resilience, as well as parenting in a digital age.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need a range of avenues in the community, virtually and physically, for parents to be supported on the ups and downs of family life in order to address the desire for privacy and the need be able to reach out widely and at scale to foster a more open culture.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to take a population health approach that addresses health inequalities and social determinants of health on the mental health of youths and ensures that the strategy is inclusive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Support for parents' mental health must also be prioritised, especially more vulnerable parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is timely that the Government is committed to promote mental health literacy, starting now at the preschool level.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We can do more to make our schools more accommodating to students' mental health needs, including at critical transition points.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The idea of support plans and accommodations based on their specific needs experienced by B in Australia and A in Singapore come to mind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There should be greater consistency in how schools acknowledge and address these challenges.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This cannot be subject to the personal ambitions or dispositions of the school leaders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must drive common understanding and best practice sharing among principals, teachers and parents.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While MOE is constantly refining the education system, we know, in our society, it will be difficult to escape a certain level of academic pressure.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But that makes it all the more important that we be very intentional in building a reservoir of positive experiences in school that students can dig into when the going gets tough.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In surveys, students say that they are most comfortable talking to their friends with their anxieties and problems, ahead of parents, teachers or school counsellors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, let us not underestimate the power of school activities that help students form friendships and be quick to dismiss them, or of making an extra effort to support the kids who sit by themselves or who have learning disabilities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are several community agencies, civil organisations and frontline staff involved in the mental health ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We know that the community is the best site for care for many.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we also know that the quality varies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even experienced doctors, teachers and social workers can miss the signs, as was in A.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can we ensure that the quality of care in the community will meet the requirements?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will we ramp up capacity fast enough?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Beyond standard processes, training and tools, how do we structure measures and incentives to drive the outcomes we want, which ultimately must be better care for our people?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Community partners I talk to also cite better collaboration with the public health system as a key enabler of better outcomes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we must also recognise that the support today is very patchy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is not clear whether this is down to the patients or the GPs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: When he lost his job, his mother-in-law belittled him and peppered him with insults like “useless idiot”.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Unfortunately, such a response is not uncommon in our community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Many older people do not have a good understanding of mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We should recognise that they are key to increasing mental health awareness.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: We should not downplay the amount of effort that is desperately needed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: If they are able to raise awareness of mental issues in their own families, we will be able to raise this awareness with more people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Our community will certainly be more supportive and more understanding towards this issue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: In other words, we can make changes from deep within our own community. : Mdm Deputy Speaker, I am not a betting person, but I would bet that every single one of us in this Chamber has had a personal brush with mental health, whether in our families, our friends or ourselves.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I have and perhaps that is why this is personal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Let us work together to create a society that is kinder and more understanding, especially for our children and youths.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: Let us work together to create a society where our children and youth know that whether it is coping with the normal stresses of life or battling more debilitating mental health conditions, they are not alone.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to speak about the importance of art-related therapies in alleviating mental health conditions; and second, I will address the mental health concerns faced by arts and cultural workers themselves.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Member, Dr Wan Rizal, in moving this Motion, briefly mentioned the role of art in wellness initiatives and I will be expanding on this idea as well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To provide some background, the term "arts therapies" is generally understood to refer to the four separate professions of music therapy, drama therapy, art therapy and dance movement therapy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Each of these arts therapies requires specialist training in their own art form and in the application of these art forms in a clinical therapeutic setting.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For ease of reference, when using the term "arts therapies" in my speech, I will be referring to the wider understanding of the term and when I refer to "art therapy" in the singular, it will be to describe the particular form of psychotherapy that helps people to effect change and growth through the use of art media and creative outlets, in a supported and safe environment.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: According to a 2022 op-ed written for Today Online by Mr Ronald Lay and Mr Lay is the programme leader of the Master's of Arts in our Therapy programme at LASALLE, 198 qualified art therapists have graduated from his programme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Art has an important part to play in both preventative and curative healthcare.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There is a whole sliding scale of uses of art for therapeutic purposes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On one end of the spectrum, you have arts as they are practised by the individual.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, quite simply put, if you or I engage in the act of, say, painting, this act of painting allows us to immerse ourselves in an activity which is meditative and contemplative.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It might allow us to momentarily lose focus on our troubles and this is an example of what is sometimes referred to as the "therapeutic value of art".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that the Government presently supports many art and cultural wellness initiatives through the good work of the National Arts Council (NAC) and the National Heritage Board (NHB), as well as their partners in the private sector.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On the other end of the spectrum, we have the notion of "art psychotherapy", and this is where a third-party professionally trained practitioner engages in a form of psychotherapy that utilises art media and creative outlets as its primary mode of expression and communication.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Art and music therapy, for example, allow participants to express themselves, when words are not enough to express their thoughts and emotions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is especially useful in cases where such participants are non-verbal or pre-verbal, and where modalities like cognitive behavioural therapy cannot work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Both curative and preventative healthcare are needed as part of a holistic approach to public health.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy 2023 advocates for with its tiered approach.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, the Strategy does not expressly mention anything about the role that the arts can play.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is in contrast to the policy positions that have been taken overseas.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This sets out specific cross-governmental programmes of work to train artists, cultural workers and healthcare workers concurrently on the design, implementation and development of cultural prescription programmes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It also raises awareness of such schemes with the public.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In Wales, Memorandums of Understanding have been signed between the Welsh National Health Service (NHS) Confederation and the Arts Council of Wales.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These set out efforts to work together for the advancement of arts, health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In September last year, I asked the Minister of Health the extent to which art therapy is included as part of HPB's initiative towards helping communities to achieve better mental health.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He replied that HPB does incorporate art-related activities, for example, mindful colouring, in their mental well-being workshops and acknowledged that "the appropriate inclusion of art, music, exercise and social interactions into our daily routine will be good for all of us." However, he also stated that evidence on the effectiveness of art therapy was said to be "still evolving." The Minister is not wrong in his focus on an evidence-based approach and, indeed, one common misconception about the field of art therapy is that its statistics and data are not as detailed or rigorous as the clinical data typically relied upon in the medical profession.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On this point, I would like to emphasise that a good deal of research is being done and has been done in the field.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The studies looked at participation in performing arts, visual arts, literature and engagement with culture and heritage.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Overall, the review concluded that the arts could have key roles to play in the prevention of ill health, the promotion of good health and the management and treatment of a range of different conditions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are many examples of studies that have been conducted in the field.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But for today’s purposes, I would like to highlight a 2017 UK report by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on Arts, Health and Well-being.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This report was issued in the UK and it spotlighted a scheme called the Artlift Arts on Prescription Scheme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This was administered in Gloucestershire County in the UK.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, health professionals referred patients with diverse mental and physical conditions to an eight-week arts programme.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A University of Gloucestershire evaluation, using the Warwick Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale, showed significant improvements in the well-being and moods of patients.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With larger sample sizes being observed in 2014 and 2017, the findings remained consistent.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This underscores the compelling impact of art-based interventions on mental health outcomes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The points I would like to communicate here are simply this.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, there are quantifiable health and cost benefits in the utilisation of art as a form of wellness and in personal artistic experiences, as well as in the field of art psychotherapy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We see this locally, from the experience of other countries and also from the research of the WHO.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These benefits support the case for a formal acknowledgement by the Government, of the arts as an important device in our arsenal of tools to promote better mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The arts and arts therapies have a key role to play in every tier of Singapore's National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Next, having identified the importance of the arts and art therapies, resources should be put in place to ensure that more relevant data is obtained, and that the practitioners of the arts therapies and arts wellness initiatives, are themselves well-supported.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We have all the basic building blocks for this in Singapore and more.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We have masters-level educational programmes in art and music therapy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We have a brand-new University of the Arts with excellent research capabilities and we have professional associations such as the Art Therapists’ Association Singapore (ATAS).

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We also have an Association of Music Therapy Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We already have entities like the Assisi Hospice, Singapore Cancer Society and various hospitals, amongst others, that not only work with our art schools but have also put in place dedicated art therapy and arts wellness programmes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are in place for their staff, patients and beneficiaries.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Our national mental wellness strategies should explicitly include these arts therapies and arts-related wellness initiatives.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I urge the Government to commit resources towards supporting our arts community in this direction.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: There are a few ways in which the support can be rendered.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, as I have said, we can dedicate more funding towards the research of arts therapies and arts wellness initiatives.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In this way, we will be able to mine more data on their efficacy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While it is possible to rely on foreign research findings, cultural specificity in data is also important.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The kinds of therapies and methods that might work in a Singapore context might not be applicable elsewhere and vice versa.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Private charities like the Red Pencil are already doing significant work in gathering data on the effects of art therapy, and their activities and those of other like them should be supported by the Government.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I would also like to urge the Government to consider engaging with the arts therapies communities to assist them, if required, in implementing some kind of formal accreditation and regulation system.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Art Therapists’ Association Singapore is one example of a non-partisan not-for-profit professional body which is run and regulated by its members.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It was established in 2008 to represent the emerging profession of art therapy in Singapore, and it seeks to advance its' members growth and development.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The view taken was that art therapy by its nature does not pose significant risk of harm to patients.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With respect, I beg to differ with the position that has been articulated by the Minister.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As explained to me by various members of the art therapist community, there is a clear difference between a situation where an individual engages in art-making or creative activities on their own for their personal enjoyment and therapeutic benefit, and a situation where a third-party practitioner uses art therapy techniques as interventions for diagnosed physical and mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister has himself observed in his reply to my PQ filed last year, these kinds of interventions should be guided by professional recommendations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Because of the lack of local regulation and accreditation, it is not necessary for people to be trained in any particular way.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I have been told anecdotally by art therapy practitioners that there can be unethical or uninformed use of art therapy by untrained persons, who may design programmes and art-based interventions intended for vulnerable populations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These include people who have diagnosed with mental health conditions or who have special needs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: When this happens, harm can be inflicted and there is no recourse for such populations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In the UK, by contrast, arts therapists are included as allied health professionals and accordingly, they are subject to a level of regulation and accountability.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here we see that regulation protects vulnerable populations, enhances confidence in the field and stimulates growth in the profession.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: That being said, I also recognise that regulation in the field of arts therapies is not a straightforward exercise.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Practitioners themselves are divided on the issue, and there is some acceptance of the idea that certain art-based interventions and modalities can be delivered well by experienced practitioners who do not have a formal post-graduate education.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, what all practitioners I have spoken to agree that the idea is that harm can be caused, and especially amongst vulnerable patients.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Minimally, frameworks should be put in place to stop this from happening.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Whether they have to do with formal frameworks of better consumer education, there are certainly steps that can be taken to protect vulnerable populations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In his 2022 op-ed for Today Online, Mr Ronald Lay rightly points out that art therapy as a discipline is relatively new in Southeast Asia and that postgraduate art therapy training at LASALLE is the only one of its kind in Singapore and in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With growing interest in the field, there is an opportunity here to create new and better jobs for our creatively inclined communities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, further professional development and support for the field of art therapies, and arts-related wellness, is something that I urge the Government to consider seriously.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Next, Mdm Deputy Speaker, I would like to address the mental health issues faced by the arts community itself.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Now, this is a community that is composed of a great number of self-employed people.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As much as we wish to consider a whole-of-Singapore effort to implement a national strategy to enhance mental health and well-being, we should not forget the specificities related to individual groups within the wider community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In a similar vein, the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy correctly identifies that an individual's mental health is not just affected by his or her own psychological well-being but is shaped by larger driving forces in society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This includes a combination of biological, social and environmental factors.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are problems that affect our arts and cultural workers in Singapore too.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The National Arts Council's Arts Resource Hub has done good work in supporting the arts community.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One of its recent projects involved hosting a gathering led by CITRUS Practices.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a group that does important work in providing free resources for the care, support and wellness of arts workers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Initiatives like this should be encouraged and supported further, ideally with funding from the Government where this is required.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While our National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy identifies the issues faced by workers in a traditional employment situation, there is scant detail on the problems faced by the self-employed.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that I had spoken about previously as well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While we seek to improve mental health and well-being for employees in a workplace environment, we should also remember to protect and respect the mental health of third-party service providers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These are service providers who may work with us on a self-employed basis or on a freelance basis.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Workers such as these may not have access to things that the rest of us take for granted, like paid medical or childcare leave.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is not right, for example, for organisations to prioritise the mental well-being of their permanent staff internally while pushing third-party service providers or freelancers to work to the point of burnout.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In order for our National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy to be effective, we must not forget the self-employed and we should ensure that positive mental wellness initiatives extend to everyone.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is almost one in five Singaporeans prone to mental health suffering.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy and today's Motion are important steps towards creating a mental health inclusive society in which every individual with a mental health challenge can feel safe to be accepted, supported and most importantly, to recover.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 2020, a survey by the Singapore Management University (SMU) showed that three in four caregivers are tired and exhausted from caring for persons with mental health issues and nine out of 10 of them require the hiring and specialised training of a domestic helper.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These caregivers can be parents, spouses or even children, depending on which stage of life that the mental health conditions afflict an individual.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Undoubtedly, caregivers of persons with mental health conditions can be bewildered and confused on what is the best course of support, especially at the onset of the mental illness in their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even for those who achieve remission, a relapse can also be very hard for their caregivers to accept and to provide support.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can imagine the emotional anxiety and physical exhaustion that they may experience resulting from having to monitor the mental conditions and physical symptoms of their loved ones and looking out for their needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By prioritising the needs of their loved ones over themselves, many caregivers can themselves fall into depression as they have to struggle with also complex emotions of anger, disappointment, exhaustion and guilt.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although there are resources available for caregivers in general, such as training programmes, support groups and counselling services, as mental illnesses can be more complex and can occur at different life stages, I would like to suggest for more tailored care and support for caregivers for persons with mental illnesses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social service agencies such as Caregivers Alliance Limited have been making remarkable contributions to these fronts, but more resources may be needed to scale caregivers' support programmes as we see the prevalence rates for mental health conditions increase.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I feel that more can be done for this group of vulnerable caregivers, especially those dealing with chronic and recurring care recipients.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would thus like to propose for the Government to enable more research and to develop strategies to address the unique needs of caregivers dealing with loved ones afflicted with recurring or chronic mental illnesses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, will the National Mental Health Competency Training Framework guide mental health practitioners in acquiring the knowledge, skills and competencies required?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can these be also extended and contextualised to family caregivers to strengthen the collaborative relationship between practitioners and caregivers of persons with mental illness?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, one of the major focuses of the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy is the expansion and improvement in access to mental health services in the primary and community settings.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the shift of mental health treatment in the community closer to home to increase care access.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By 2030, this will be extended to more polyclinics, including new ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is certainly a step in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, in Singapore, a substantial portion of primary care family doctors are operating out of private GP clinics.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Several of my Jalan Kayu residents shared with me that GP clinics are often more convenient and perceived as less stigmatising for them to approach for mental health challenges concerns, as compared to the mental health section of polyclinics or even psychiatric wards of public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the ease and costs of receiving both medication and counselling intervention in the primary and community settings still have their gaps as they may be delivered by different professionals from different organisations at different locations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For an individual with early onset of mental challenge symptoms like prolonged insomnia and low moods and clinically diagnosed for depression and/or anxiety, he or she may benefit from the counselling therapy as the first line of treatment and some medication from a GP.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, he or she is unlikely to receive both care at the same GP clinic at the same time, especially for the counselling therapy component.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If they need a certain type of prescription medication not carried by the GP, this will also pose some difficulties in their access to the needed care.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Counselling therapy sessions in the private setting also usually cost more than in polyclinics or public hospitals.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Usually, individuals facing mental health challenges are already scared, overwhelmed and in distress when diagnosed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such fee gradients and wait-time between medication and counselling at their GP private clinics in the neighbourhood versus public polyclinics and hospitals' psychiatric wards may increase patients' psychological burdens and disrupt treatment follow-up.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government can elaborate on more plans and protocols to manage the cost and facilitate the referral and provision of both medication and counselling therapy in the primary and community care settings.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, I wish to address the need for employers and co-workers to understand accommodation needed by individuals with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We know that while work is essential for economic and social reasons, it can be challenging for those affected by mental illness to sustain employment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Studies in Europe have shown that, although most persons with severe mental illness are willing to seek competitive employment, they are nevertheless substantially excluded from the workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To better support persons with mental health conditions, workplace intervention and accommodation is necessary to help those who desire employment, which will allow them to achieve financial independence and security, contributing to their sense of belonging to a community and boosting their self-confidence and positive identity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to know that one of the Government's key focuses in the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy, is on improving workplace mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This includes enhancing mental well-being in the workplace, tackling workplace discrimination and strengthening employment support for individuals with mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also encouraged by the moves of various companies in the private sector that has introduced flexible work arrangements and welfare policies to support the mental well-being of employees with differing needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that helping persons with mental illness seek or stay in employment, is an important part of mental health intervention to be incorporated in their care and treatment plan.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, stigma and discrimination inevitably continue to exist within some workplaces.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It should not be a surprise that such common mental health conditions are included in the Chronic Disease Management Programme in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because, they are, unfortunately, often chronic in nature.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have heard of stories of inclusive work teams who, out of good intentions, had thought that helping a colleague with mental health condition to discontinue medication is a sign towards recovery, just to be shocked to see their colleague suffer a relapse after a high workload period.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather, it is a state of well-being in which an individual can realise his or her abilities and potential to work productively and make contributions to the society.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today's Motion and the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy are a commitment to the holistic well-being of every Singaporean.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a pledge to foster a society where mental health is no longer seen as a stigma, but as part of a nation's collective responsibility.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our nation starts incorporating mental health as a key pillar of our healthcare policy, I believe that as a united people, we can work together to build a more resilient, compassionate and mentally healthy Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding my considerations raised, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is no secret that Singapore and Singaporeans are stressed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Another study from the National Youth Council (NYC) and the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) Social Lab, found our young people and young workers experiencing high levels of burnout and that their mental well-being had still not fully recovered from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Union leaders, too, have told me that their fellow colleagues, across all workforce segments – rank and file, PMEs and freelancers – are highly stressed at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
