text: The main reason cited was how it is almost impossible to disconnect from work when we live in a hyper-connected and global world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must, therefore, do more to prevent, identify and treat mental health-related issues at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The strategy aims to create an effective mental health ecosystem, comprising accessible and good quality clinical care, with a supportive community and society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Instead of an over-emphasis on mental disorders, the Government has recognised that the state of mental well-being is intertwined with a supportive community.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And I argue that our workplaces, where most of us spend most of our waking hours, must form a key part of societal support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need strong upstream measures to address workplace mental health stresses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since I first mooted the idea of the right to disconnect in this House in 2020, several countries have moved ahead with their own versions of the right to disconnect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Belgium passed a law in February 2022 that allowed civil servants to disconnect after hours without a fear of reprisals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Closer to home, the Philippines is debating a Bill that seeks to give workers the right to disconnect after work hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Locally, union leaders have told me that there are exemplary practices at the company level that provide workers with the ability to switch off after work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am glad that senior public sector leaders in MOM and MOH, just to name a couple of examples, have made it a point to tell staff that they do not need to feel obligated to respond to emails or work messages sent after work hours, unless it is expressly marked as urgent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should make this workplace culture the norm rather than the exception.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In November 2020, we published the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at Workplaces that set out practical guidance on measures that employers can adopt to support their employees' mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Advisory also called on employers to recognise the need for staff to have adequate rest outside work hours, in recognition that the work-from-home arrangement had blurred the lines between work and personal life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The tripartite partners further refresh the Tripartite Advisory on Mental Well-being at Workplaces in 2023 to include the setting up of a peer-support system to help employers create a supportive environment for employees in need and to de-stigmatise mental health issues at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These examples show that the close working relationship between the Labour Movement, the Government and the employers have resulted in successful and tangible measures that have helped to advance mental health outcomes at the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But let us work and agree on a set of Tripartite Guidelines that establish principles on, what a right to disconnect could mean for different sectors and for different job roles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: After a few years, we could then review how effective the guidelines are and to consider further action, including legislation, if necessary at the point of time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Standing Order 2 expressly states that, Parliamentary proceedings shall be interrupted at 7.00 pm, unless the Leader of the House moves a business Motion to extend the day's Sitting beyond that moment of interruption.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: After all, Members should be accorded ample time to rest and to recharge and to prepare for the next day's Sitting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: On this, I am sure that all Members would not disagree with me.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We only have 24 hours in a day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Lack of adequate downtime can lead to job burnout, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is, therefore, crucial for individuals to re-evaluate our approach to work and life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By prioritising, focusing and scheduling downtime, we can reduce stress, enhance our creativity, improve our productivity and, more importantly, lead a healthier and more balanced life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to disconnecting after work, we need to have trained personnel at the workplace that can identify and do basic triage of early mental health symptoms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Deploying such trained mental health ambassadors at the workplace can help employers maintain a well-adjusted and mentally healthy workforce, thereby ensuring high levels of productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Union leaders can play this important role of mental health ambassadors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, NTUC has trained over 1,700 union leaders in workplace safety and health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And the Labour Movement stands ready to partner with our tripartite partners in training and deploying mental health ambassadors at all workplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This course is WSQ-certified and supported by the WSH Council and, I encourage all youths to sign up for this course to become a peer supporter.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is now commonplace to read about company retrenchments, due to restructuring and cutbacks.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Recent examples include Alphabet, Amazon and Lazada, which show that even the workers in growth sectors, such as technology and e-commerce, are not spared.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They are men and women who must deal with a sudden loss of income and a disrupted career.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some may feel a deep embarrassment about being retrenched, even if the layoffs were unrelated to their own work performance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Layoffs also affect the "surviving" employees within the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Those who are retained often take on an immense amount of additional workload and they constantly wonder if they will be the next to get laid off.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I, therefore, hope that companies can recognise that retrenchments should be done as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, what can employers do to limit the psychological impact of a retrenchment exercise?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, communication should come from the top, with the leadership team owning the message.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But it also needs to be a two-way process, allowing all employees to have their questions answered.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, every impacted group needs support that is tailored to their needs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Providing more generous compensation packages for retrenched workers can help to alleviate immediate financial concerns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Employers can work with NTUC on job placements and training for new job roles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, employers need to think carefully about job redesign and workload distribution for the remaining roles of those who are left behind in the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Retrenchments are never pleasant, but there are ways for employers to undertake the process with compassion and to treat all employees – whether they are staying or leaving – with utmost dignity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Companies which retrench irresponsibly should not be let off the hook for the stress and mental trauma that they cause.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, more can be done to improve the affordability of mental healthcare.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also grow the industry and increase capacity to reduce waiting times.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Assurance must also be given to employees that their confidentiality is protected and it would not affect their personnel records with the company.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge more companies to adopt EAP services and to engage credible EAP service providers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement has and will continue to help drive the adoption of EAP services at workplaces to safeguard workers’ mental health.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It was recently reported that the findings from the 2022 Quality of Life Survey found that Singaporeans have become less happy over the past decade, despite real incomes rising over this period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Even high net worth individuals in Singapore are found to be concerned with their work-life balance, according to a recent study reported in The Business Times.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mental health issues at the workplace affect everyone, regardless of socioeconomic status and designation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to tip the balance and advance mental health outcomes at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must prevent workplace burnout by doing more for workers to have the right to disconnect.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should train and deploy workplace mental wellness ambassadors to help identify early mental health challenges and, where necessary, we certainly need a proliferation of EAP providers to treat and to address mental health challenges.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I appreciate Dr Wan Rizal and fellow Parliamentarians' initiative of putting forth this Motion.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: A 2022 survey on the well-being of small business owners by global small business platform, Xero, revealed a startling paradox.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Other data points that made me sit up: 39% were taskmasters who found it hard to take a break from work, while 41% expressed a low sense of fulfilment from work.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Driven by a constant sense of responsibility and duty to their business, it is inevitable that many small business owners work intensive hours in intense focus.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The pool includes freelancers and self-employed persons, a less visible group of our Singapore workforce, whom my fellow NMP Ms Usha Chandradas also spoke about.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For brevity, I will refer to them as freelancers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Spurred on by pandemic fears and financial losses and challenged by the increasingly uncertain business outlook, freelancers as diverse as photographers, sports coaches and private hire vehicle drivers have been working relentlessly to rebuild their confidence, business and savings.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many are now feeling overworked and burnt out.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In my capacity as a labour representative, I would like to give voice to the concerns of three groups of freelancers who are hard-hit by internal and external stressors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They are the platform workers, working caregivers and mature-age small business owners.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I would also suggest three approaches that could contribute to improving their mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: What is more worrying is that while nearly two-thirds surveyed professed resilience to the uncertainties of platform work, this is not reflected in their state of health.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because of global challenges and inflation, platform workers expect operating costs to continue to rise.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, many worry that their incomes are not keeping pace.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is because job allocation and trip fares are at the mercy of the black box algorithm of platform operators.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The upcoming changes in legislation are intended to better protect platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, it is only if the changes are reinforced by shared responsibility of the tripartite of Government, platform worker associations and platform operators can these changes translate to positive outcomes of sustainable livelihood and improved well-being of platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To platform workers, sustainable livelihood means knowing that for the same amount of work done, they will receive consistent, transparent and fair compensation, and not inconsistent and fluctuating amounts, whilst improved well-being means giving platform workers the assurance that platform operators’ pursuit of profit and returns to shareholders are not at the expense of platform workers’ health and safety.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I echo the platform workers’ hope for a brighter tomorrow as we await the new legislation to come onstream this year.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The same IPS study revealed that 46% of the platform drivers and riders surveyed were unable to find other work due to personal reasons, such as caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, a condition such as dementia impacts more than those living with the condition.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Dementia affects about one in 10 in Singapore aged 60 and above.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This number is set to rise as Singapore ages.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The CEO of Dementia Singapore, Jason Foo, shared in a 2022 The Straits Times article: "For every person with dementia, one or two family caregivers have to change their entire lifestyle, or give up work, to care for the person with dementia".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I know of individuals who switched to freelancing because of caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I know, too, of freelancers who dialled back on work because of caregiving duties.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This suggests a need for an inclusive, enlightened and supportive ecosystem for freelancers with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers who are caregivers should be uplifted and supported with the same degree of accommodation and care as what we seek for employees with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In respect of the freelancer ecosystem, I would like to ask that service buyers and platform operators give leeway in service delivery or incentive framework if the freelancer or platform worker must respond urgently to caregiving emergencies.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, care facilities, such as hospitals and homes, could extend consideration to freelancers who are juggling caregiving and income-earning responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some freelancers shared their frustrating experiences when liaising with different agencies and facilities that, in turn, have different levels of empathy and responsiveness to these freelancers in need.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to relate the experience of Ms T, a private hire car driver and sole breadwinner.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Ms T found herself stranded after a second fall at home worsened her aged mother's injury.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Ms T sought help from the social worker when she found it challenging trying to juggle the logistics and finances of caring for her mother at home while trying to make ends meet driving.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Ms T was told by the social worker that Ms T’s mother did not qualify for subsidised nursing home care.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: When Ms T tried to find out the reason for rejection, she was ignored.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Ms T was left feeling stranded, stressed, tired and helpless.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers, such as Ms T, feel they are held hostage to unproductive and frustrating processes.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They find themselves unable to assert their need for empathy and expedience and thus, suffer in silence.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers with caregiving responsibilities would benefit from an integrated approach to supporting care recipients and their caregivers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This entails a whole-of-nation commitment to build an inclusive, enlightened and supportive ecosystem.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Xero study of small business owners found that Singapore’s small business owners under age 30 had higher overall well-being levels than those over 50.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This could be a consequence of rapid digitalisation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The acceleration of digitalisation during the pandemic compelled businesses to adapt to new consumer demands.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many from this group are financially stretched to part with funds upfront for updated software and technology.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Mature freelancers who are trying hard to cope with the pace of change while overcoming the digital divide by upskilling would certainly appreciate targeted and sustained funding support from the Government.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Circling back to the same Xero survey, Singapore’s small business owners ranked second in terms of overall well-being and life satisfaction.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, despite the challenges, freelancers are generally optimistic about the future.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I had earlier shared the stresses of three groups of freelancers, in particular, platform workers, working caregivers and mature small business owners.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I had also suggested three approaches to uplift their mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to recap how, as a whole-of-nation, we could provide the solidarity and support to improve freelancers’ mental health and well-being.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, stakeholders could commit to a shared responsibility towards freelancers’ well-being.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, a national level commitment to build an inclusive, enlightened and supportive ecosystem to support freelancers with caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This empowers mature freelancers with the confidence and ability to strive for sustainable business and longevity of livelihood.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These three approaches can be the game-changers for platform workers, freelancers with caregiving needs and mature freelancers in Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They give freelancers and self-employed persons the confidence to pursue professional progress and personal happiness as viable intertwined priorities and could be practical next steps in the articulation of this Motion.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I am also a member of WG3 that contributed toward the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The onset can take us totally by surprise or can be the result of life's challenges.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It can be triggered at home, in school and at work by an emotional experience or a bereavement.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must reduce barriers and increase entry points to help-seeking.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This makes supporting help-seeking for our under-18s critical.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged that the Government is presently reviewing the age of consent for youths to access counselling or therapy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Common law states 21 as the age of consent, while some local mental health providers generally require parental consent to serve those under 18.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But requiring parental consent, whether at age 18 or 21, discourages help-seeking in many youths.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some do not want their parents to know at the onset, especially if parents are unsupportive.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some fear disappointing their parents or believe it would further burden their already burdened parents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There are also instances where parents have declined medication for their child simply because of stigma.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Youths aged 14 to 16 report more serious symptoms than those other youths with depression and anxiety.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Mental health support must be readily accessible for our youths from 14 to 18 years old.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For this group, may I ask the Government to consider tiered guidelines for the types of mental health services that would or would not require parental consent?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For example, access to mental health screening, assessment or basic counselling could be tier 1 services not requiring parental consent.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This supports the good work many youth counselling agencies are already doing.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Tier 2 services requiring parental consent could include interventions requiring medication, hospital admissions or surgical procedures.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Where parents are deemed absent or unwilling to make decisions beneficial for the child, MSF could be invited to step in on behalf of the child or the Gillick Competency Test can be applied by a certified clinician.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, it is vital we protect our 14- to below 18-year-olds from errant mental health practitioners.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This leads to my next point: proper licensing of mental health practitioners serving youths.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we upgrade the capabilities of our mental health service providers, we need to ensure proper certification and licensing of professional mental health service providers, particularly those who list themselves as psychologists, counsellors and therapists.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is crucial for those who treat youths below 18.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Presently, the only mental health practitioners that are properly regulated are psychiatrists, who fall under the purview of the Singapore Medical Council.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Anyone can refer to themselves as a therapist or counsellor.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To ensure the safety of our youths, mental health services they have access to should be regulated and licensed.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There must be strong disciplinary consequences to violations of professional conduct and ethics.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will perhaps ease the concerns of our parents and also promote safe help-seeking behaviours in our youths.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In our work at Trybe, a youth non-governmental organisation (NGO), we observe an increasing trend in youths educating themselves on mental wellness via social media resources.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some sources have been particularly helpful, supporting our youths in their mental wellness journey, but some have provided inaccurate or incomplete information.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We have youths telling our counsellors, "I know you are using CBT on me, and I know the next question you're about to ask", or "I want another therapy approach".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This view of believing that they know what CBT, short for Cognitive Behavioural Therapy, or any one approach, is all about is an inaccurate view of therapy as a whole.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Different therapy approaches are not a menu meant to fit personal preferences alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Good therapists draw on various techniques and tools to meet the client's needs at different points of the therapy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Such information on social media can create mistaken notions of what therapy is, when actually, if approached consistently, would bring out the best results for the client.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Social media has become and will continue to be a regular source of information and news for our youths.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We should continue to leverage social media to support youths in their mental wellness journey as there remains many positive influences.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But to reduce misinformation, the Government could explore co-curating a list of social media accounts on mental wellness together with our youths, validating accounts recommended by our youths themselves.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I was heartened to hear that HPB conducts Mental Wellness Skills Equipping Programmes addressing life transition years from preschool to Primary 1 as well as Primary 6 to Secondary 1.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I would also like to propose that the Government look into the transition years of Secondary 2 to Secondary 3.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The pressure at this transitional stage stems from various reasons: the increased pressure and workload due to the approaching "O" levels, the adjustments to new classmates from streaming, and greater awareness of one's sexuality, relationship and identity issues.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Others active in their CCAs are given increased leadership responsibilities when the Secondary 4 students step down from their positions, all these while navigating in these formative years.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A more in-depth survey could be done to gain further insights on this unique transitional age for our Singapore students.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we develop resources for school intervention programmes, might we consider a more collaborative approach with our youths?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the UK, in preparation for Children's Mental Health Week, the team gathers feedback from primary and secondary students on what and how they would like to learn about mental health in school.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Downloadable resources are then developed for students from four-year-olds to 18-year-olds, to facilitate conversations during mental health week in families and in schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Two interesting findings from the feedback were received: first, getting students to lead lessons on mental health; and second, for school assemblies on the topic to be short and engaging.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The resources are used in over 500 schools across the UK and downloaded over 200,000 times in 2022 alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Who knows what we may uncover as we work together with our youths for their mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: HPB's Youth Preventive Health and Dental Services conducts annual health screening for our students in primary and secondary schools.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, the Youth Integrated Team (YIT) also conducts mental health screening for youths at risk of mental illnesses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This supports early intervention and normalises mental health discussions at school-going age for our students and parents.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The issue of lack of insurance coverage for people with mental illness has been raised by several Members last year, specifically, the challenge in obtaining insurance for physical health conditions outside of the mental illness individuals have or used to have.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This gap impedes help-seeking behaviours in adults who may not afford treatment without the support of insurance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A psychiatrist friend related how patients have requested to be officially discharged or not to be treated at all, just so they can purchase physical health insurance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In one case, a patient's financial consultant shared with him that buying accident and health insurance would be impossible if he remained on medication.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam had responded in Parliament that those wishing to top up subsidised services and MediShield Life may do so via private insurers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These insurers are expected not to indiscriminately reject an application based solely on declared information, including mental health conditions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, such incidents happen in far greater frequency than reported.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In a published interview from 2020, Ms Linda Lui reported that after fully recovering from a field accident as an army cadet, she experienced post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This happened a year after she returned to civilian life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: And as she sought therapy in a Government institute, her doctors advised her not to disclose her PTSD diagnosis because it would complicate things and affect the insurance coverage she had bought prior to the diagnosis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: She states, "I chose to remain silent about my mental health in order to protect my physical health".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The fear expressed by her and her doctors are not unfounded.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In another published interview, Ms Vas shared how countless insurance companies denied her applications to be insured against critical illness and hospitalisation on account of her bipolar disorder diagnosis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is even after her doctor certified her physically healthy and compliant to her medications.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In her interview, Ms Vas also revealed the multiple appeal letters made to various insurance companies, including an appeal by her MP.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These appeals only add mental load to their already mentally burdened state.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Given ongoing examples of rejection, coupled by warnings from doctors and insurance brokers not to declare their illnesses, one's options are to conceal, skip treatment or go without insurance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There are private insurers that do insure those with mental illnesses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, their premiums are often unaffordable for the masses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Individuals recovering or have recovered from mental illness should not be penalised for boldly seeking help for their mental health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Yet, the discrimination against people recovering or have recovered from mental illness when obtaining insurance for physical health conditions can be daunting.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Mental health clinics often operate during work hours and weekend slots get filled very quickly.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This means when an individual needs to seek mental health support on a weekday, they would need to take leave from work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Individuals then hesitate to seek treatment due to their limited annual leave and the risk of it being known that they are seeing a mental health professional.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some companies have implemented a 14-day well-being leave in place of the traditional medical leave.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It allows staff to take leave for physical or mental illness for when their dependants require care or to take time-off for their own personal well-being, all without the need for medical certification.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This benefits parents, caregivers and individuals across a broad spectrum.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will meet the evolving needs of Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Third, mental health check-ups in national health screening.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But if we abandon injured people, there will be no resilience".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By reducing institutional barriers and increasing entry points to help-seeking, we will show up meaningfully for the individuals in need, raising the resilience of our people and society.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A topic of national significance requires a collective effort to achieve our shared objective.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is not just a medical issue, but a national and social one.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Even for us "kiasu" Singaporeans, this is probably not the statistic we are most proud of.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In my line of work, a fast-paced demanding working life is also my personal experience.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For many adult Singaporeans, a majority of their waking hours is spent working.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: With digitalisation, now augmented by artificial intelligence, more will be demanded of workers than ever before.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday's work-life balance has become today's work-life integration.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial then that the mental well-being of Singaporeans has to be looked after at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that our national strategy, under focus area 4, recognises this clearly.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike larger corporations, SMEs generally do not include mental health coverage in their medical benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: With tighter budgets and limited human resources, SMEs are more cautious in structuring their employee mental health benefits, preferring to start with basic inclusions, like having a 24/7 counselling hotline.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, multinational corporations (MNCs) have more at their disposal.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Employee Assistance Programmes (EAPs), third-party vendor-led sessions and mental health toolkits are not uncommon finds at leading MNCs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While there has been a sharp increase in companies including mental health coverage from 2020 to 2023, MNCs are mostly behind driving this.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To encourage such companies to implement well-being programmes and mental health coverage, the cost of adoption must be reduced.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Digital tools are now able to provide objective data on the mental health landscape of an organisation using employee self-assessments.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Tripartite Advisory on Mental Health and Well-being at Workplaces recommends organisations to use iWorkHealth, a digital self-administered tool, to understand the general state of employee well-being.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A few hon Members who spoke before me have also mentioned this useful tool.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Other national level digital tools such as MindSG, Mindline and Let’s Talk, are also highlighted in the Mental Health Strategy Report.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While these tools are a step in the right direction, there is a need to find more innovative ways to encourage SMEs to leverage technologies or platforms that help them better understand and support employee well-being in a cost-effective way.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Well-meaning SMEs looking to advance their mental health support often find themselves constrained by a lack of expertise.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Under the Total WSH Programme by the WSH Council, companies will be paired with Total WSH Service Providers who will work with them to assess health, mental well-being and safety risks in the workplace before introducing specific interventions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A programme like this has the potential to amplify the mental health resources available to SMEs, in a consistent and scalable manner.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Government share an update on whether this programme has been successful, and what more can be done to encourage SMEs to participate?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: What were some of the learnings, workplace adjustments or best practices that companies can easily adopt?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Would it be feasible for MOM and WSH Council to expand grant coverage to include consultancy costs, so that SMEs can better deliver the "how to" in addition to the "what to" on the mental health matters?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: On average, they range between 1% and 3%.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It would be insightful to understand how the Public Service Division’s EAPs compare.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Low utilisation rate in the private sector can be attributed to a lack of trust towards companies, stigma around calling a counsellor and unconvincing communication regarding the benefits of EAPs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Tripartite Advisory on Well-Being at Workplaces recommends that companies assure employees that conversations with EAP providers will be kept confidential.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is absolutely critical to ensure that EAPs are used at all.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Addressing mental health concerns within the workplace requires confidentiality, support, and the eradication of stigma.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is especially important for those grappling with chronic mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A 2021 study showed that only six in 10 respondents were willing to work with someone with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This shows that stigma is still at large.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The long-term hidden nature of chronic mental health conditions requires ongoing support and more understanding.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For someone with these conditions, to disclose or not to disclose is a real dilemma.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given this, the upcoming Workplace Fairness Legislation, which recognises mental health as a "protected characteristic", is highly relevant.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For employees and employers alike to navigate this new landscape confidently, clarity is essential.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government clarify how this legislation will protect employees who choose to disclose their mental health conditions or even invisible disabilities?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: How will it guarantee that such disclosures result in genuine support and prevent any form of further stigma or discrimination?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Such clarifications will go a long way to enable those who need help, to seek the right support.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Improper handling of mental health disclosures creates an environment where employees may hesitate to seek help due to fears of repercussions or discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Someone once shared with me a real conversation they had at an SME.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When they sought support for mental health concerns, the response from their manager was dismissive: "Don't tell me.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If you want help, tell HR and have it on your record." When an employee discloses their mental health condition to their supervisor, there is also an implicit expectation of confidentiality, if not support.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When this information is further freely shared with senior management or other employees without consent or regard, trust is eroded, giving rise to the impression that open disclosure can be punished.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Such fears or lack of trust cannot be allowed to fester, for it is trust and psychological safety that make up the foundation of a truly inclusive and supportive workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the public sector, the Government has a significant opportunity to play a leading role in promoting the normalisation of working with individuals facing mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This will help us gain valuable insights into the effectiveness of current support measures, helping us understand what has worked and what has not.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Government initiatives such as the well-being champions network tap on managers to identify signs of burnout and stress among employees.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Some companies have also trained mental health first aiders to create a peer support network.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I have personally heard stories where workplace peers were able to spot an employee showing signs of distress, signs even their family missed.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While trained managers and peers play a key role in workplace well-being, it is essential to acknowledge that they do not replace expert help.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When addressing workplace mental health, we must not forget that they shoulder an emotional burden in the service of others, on top of their regular workload.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on from the workplace, I would also like to touch on the more vulnerable groups in our society before I close.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When addressing disability, we cannot focus on just the medical dimension alone.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must not neglect the mental health risk that comes with feelings of limitation, lack of agency or loneliness.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, it is common for mental health conditions like depression to accompany those who acquire disability in adulthood, as they navigate profound adjustments to a new reality.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Living with chronic or severe illnesses is emotionally challenging.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The demands of managing the chronic physical condition may lead to the failure to spot mental health symptoms, both by doctor and patient, during clinic visits.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Developing personalised mental health plans that address the emotional aftermath of illness is essential for a patient’s long-term well-being.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It would be helpful to know if the Government will consider this when implementing our mental health strategy.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The unpredictability of life means we cannot discount the possibility that any one of us could acquire disability or significant health challenges in future, especially as we age.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In our national approach, we must strive for authentic solutions and stay well clear of well-being washing.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When we do this well, I am positive that every Singaporean will benefit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But beyond dollars and cents, mental health conditions are often deeply painful and cost individuals years of lost hope, fractured relationships with care partners and family who are unable to cope with the strain, ending of careers as their lives spiral into a form they do not recognise and feelings like stress and guilt as they struggle to cope on the surface.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, this lasts a lifetime and recovery is not linear.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Cheng San-Seletar, student volunteers, corporate partners, grassroots leaders and agency representatives commemorate World Mental Health Day every October.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We host a campaign incorporating self-care activities, nature and opportunities to form social networks among neighbours and friends.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the first day, we door knock more than 18,000 households to ask "How Are You?" checks on our residents and share access to mental health resources.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The idea is to reach in and start a conversation on mental health in the community because mental health illnesses can be incredibly isolating and lonely, and it is not always easy to take the first step to seek help.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our message is that you are not alone and that we are here for you.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Efforts continue for the rest of the year, working with community partners, including through our Calm Corners, which are rolled out at void decks in every zone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the work to raise awareness and increase outreach is only a start.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened by the launch of the National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy by the Inter-agency Taskforce, and I am supportive of the four focus areas.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am also grateful for all healthcare workers and many different individuals whose work has brought us here.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The efforts in the strategy will take significant effort and resources, not just from Government but also from the different sectors, private sector as well as all of society in tackling stigma and creating a culture of care.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will also take time, and I note that the National Mental Health Office is likely to only be established by 2025.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But Sir, the issues are pressing here and now, and we must tackle them with haste.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And Singapore recorded more suicides across all age groups in 2022, with a significant increase amongst the elderly and youth populations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, I will raise three key points on access and affordability to mental health treatment and support, caring for the mental health of our seniors and support for vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While readiness to do so is, indeed, the first step, we must also consider the financial capacity of such individuals and the ease at which they can access mental health support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Past surveys have also cited high cost as a deterrent, resulting in a treatment gap which often leads to mental health conditions worsening over time.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there are helplines and some free counselling sessions available, long-term dedicated care and medication can cost patients hundreds or even over $1,000 per visit.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This leads us to a crucial point – the Government's role in shaping the insurance market to promote affordable and accessible mental health coverage, as well as general health and hospitalisation coverage for everyday Singaporeans facing mental health challenges.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is already tough enough for individuals facing mental challenges to get through their daily life, many of whom have to stop work and are faced with difficulties when asked to declare whether they have gone through or are currently facing mental health challenges, as they try to sign up for even simple hospitalisation insurance to try and avoid further financial stress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Underwriting coverage for mental illnesses is complex given the diverse ways these disorders impact individuals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As several hon Members in this House, including just two before me, Miss Rachel Ong, have urged the Government to do more in this front, I will spare Members' well-being and not repeat the same points but I, too, reiterate this call to Government, as well as private insurers and would like to just ask if the Government has considered encouraging private insurers to launch innovative, affordable insurance products and if the Government has considered mental health parity laws to prohibit health plans from imposing barriers on access to mental health.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike youth mental well-being and health, there are few community organisations or ground-up groups which focus on supporting the mental health needs of seniors and, given our ageing population, I call on the Government to do more in this area.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chronic health conditions, reduced mobility, retirement, empty nests and the passing of close friends – these are just some of the difficult moments that our seniors go through as time passes on.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, digital transformation and a built environment, unlike the kampongs they grew up in, often feel alienating.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While efforts to destigmatise mental health conditions and encourage help-seeking behaviours are well-intentioned, some seniors expressed difficulty discussing mental health as it is considered taboo.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With a tiered care model, the provision of care is shared with community partners with trained personnel on the ground.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, staff are often stretched, managing many cases.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must encourage everyone to be eyes and ears, equip ourselves with knowledge and destigmatise early screening and help-seeking as the norm to provide timely interventions for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my constituency, community partners such as the mailmen and women from Sing Post monitor changes in mail collection patterns in blocks with a high number of elderly and participating hawkers are trained to recognise simple signs of depression and dementia before referring seniors to the nearest Active Ageing Centre (AAC) or our community clubs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the biggest threats to our seniors' well-being is social isolation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not only seniors who live alone who experience loneliness.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a study on social disconnection and its impact on the health of older adults by the NUS, the findings found that most socially disconnected individuals are living with family members.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In another research by the Centre for Ageing Research and Education, a significant percentage of older Singaporeans staying in multi-generational households indicated feeling lonely.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These trends could stem from poor familial relationships or the lack of interaction between family members, as everyone is busy with their lives or on their digital devices.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On this note, how can adult children and grandchildren be better equipped with skills to talk about mental health with seniors?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond immediate family, how can wider community initiatives and befrienders reaching out to seniors to reassure them and encourage participation in community efforts?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, I understand Age Well SG will scale up the quality and quantity of AACs to increase meaningful engagement with our seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Silver Generation Office also does good work.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are reaching out to seniors at greater risk of isolation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is likely to naturally engage the more active seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the efforts in place for seniors who are isolated or already experiencing mental health issues and how will efforts and resources, such as COMIT, be better resourced under the strategy?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It deeply saddened our community when we lost some of our elderly residents to suicide, especially during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the task force will consider developing a more targeted approach for seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On my final point, I echo the points raised by hon Member Mr Ong Hua Han.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Persons with disabilities are not only more likely to experience mental distress but also factors associated with a higher occurrence of mental health conditions, including financial stress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This intersectionality of disability, socioeconomic factors and healthcare access plays a pivotal role in shaping mental health outcomes within the Singaporean context.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Key measures should include ensuring that screening, care and support services are not only accessible but tailored to the unique needs of this population.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a dearth in specialist healthcare for persons with disabilities, especially in our heartlands.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond Government policies to promote inclusivity, efforts by employers and wider society aimed at enhancing educational and employment opportunities and fostering an open environment are essential towards reducing disparities and creating access.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is mental health included in health education lessons, for example, in our special needs schools?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mental health challenges affect all levels of society, both young and old.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, we should speak more about mental well-being in our normal conversations, especially when it concerns our senior citizens who may feel lonely.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apart from being patient with them and praying for them, we should be tactful when giving advice and words of encouragement to those in need.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can also persuade and help them to seek advice from specialists, such as counselling and therapy, or to get enough medication.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should not feel embarrassed to seek support because such prompt assistance can help to save jobs, family or even the lives of loved ones.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, they are not seeking our advice or expertise to solve their problems.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They simply need a friend to pour their hearts out to. : Finally, Sir, alongside strategies to improve service coordination and care systems, we must consider local training and education pathways and spaces for professionals, such as clinical psychiatrists, to help the system cope with increased load, even as we move beyond tackling mental health crises to upstream intervention.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Further, as we encourage peer support, clarity on the qualifications and certifications necessary for practitioners or peer supporters at various tiers besides the expected relevant skills and knowledge will be helpful.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is well and good to say that it is okay not to be okay.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But think about perhaps the neighbour below who says they hear noises coming from your house and cannot control their emotions, lashing out at you in the corridor.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Consider the hoarder, who perhaps arrived at this state because of the loss of loved ones years ago and has unprocessed trauma.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Imagine a loved one, who was always a pillar of support for you, but now cannot get out of bed on the bad days.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the end of the day, it is true understanding, empathy and recognition that counts and can make a difference in someone's mental health journey.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us be mindful of the language and terms that we use and let us be kind to one another, especially when it is hard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By many indicators, the mental health status of an increasing number of Singaporeans is low and getting worse every year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The situation is even worse for our young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The same data shows that approximately 25% of those living with a mental illness are between 18 and 29 years of age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These figures tell us that approximately one in six Singaporeans is currently living with a mental illness of some sort and that one in four of those are young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The same data shows that suicide is the leading cause of death for people between 10 and 29 years of age, accounting for almost one in every three deaths in this age group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As a social worker and counsellor, I am distressed but not surprised by this data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Life is tough for many people, including many young people, and it is getting tougher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The impact of social media, climate change, global insecurity and uncertain employment, housing and relationship options present a bleak picture for many.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Suicide appears to be increasingly commonplace and this is deeply distressing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I have seen first-hand the impact that suicide can have on partners, friends, colleagues, even strangers, and I have recently witnessed the impact on my own children following the suicide of a long-term friend of theirs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am also pleased to note that our Government is strengthening our existing mental health frameworks by developing the National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy, a strategy that I support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: My comments fall into three areas targeted at accessible mental health services, suitability to practice and workplace mental health and well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: WHO defines vulnerable populations as, and I quote, "Those who, due to factors usually considered outside their control, do not have the same opportunities as other, more fortunate groups in society." There are many causes of vulnerability, including physical, social, cultural, economic and environmental factors, all of which can make it difficult for certain groups of people to access appropriate mental health services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, children, young people, the elderly, women, men, migrant workers, those under the care of others, people living with a disability, or living in poverty, or who are unemployed, or, somewhat ironically, people living with a mental illness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: All of these people, in fact, all Singaporeans, can sometimes face barriers to not only recognising that they need assistance, but also seeking assistance and then accessing the appropriate care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is important that the Government also works closely with the private and community sectors and, importantly, with people of all ages, backgrounds and capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important that we do not simply introduce more and more services but that we acknowledge and address existing and emerging factors that increase vulnerability and are an impediment to positive mental health and well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In essence, mental health extends beyond the mere absence of mental disorders and is intrinsic to overall quality of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is one of the safest countries in the world, has an exceptional education and health system and offers world-class sport and recreation opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, as the National Population Health Survey and SOS data I referenced earlier indicates, this is clearly not enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Something is missing and many of our children are struggling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, essential to remember that the difficulties that many of our children are experiencing, are not a reflection of their own character, resilience or strength but a reflection of the world in which they live.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: ACEs are potentially traumatic events that occur in childhood and can include experiencing violence, abuse or neglect; growing up in a family with mental health or substance use problems; witnessing violence in the home; living in poverty or insecure housing; chronic unemployment; parental separation; or household members being in prison.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: ACEs are correlated with future chronic health problems, mental illness and substance use problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: ACEs can also negatively impact education, job opportunities, earning potential and future relationships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For this group, we need to consider a holistic systemic approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just about providing mental health services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to consider what more can be done to alleviate ACEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot eliminate all factors, but we can do more to identify and mitigate these risk factors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to create an environment where individuals can access the services they need, when they need them, without any perceived or actual stigma, adverse consequences or reprisals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do more to make Singapore a community where children can safely say to their parents, their friends and their teachers that they are struggling; that they are not ok.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, with a coordinated and sustained effort by the Government, private and community sectors, we can get there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While this is positive, in that it suggests that young people are becoming more willing to ask for help, it is still alarming that so many young people feel they need mental health support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Everything and anything we do, from designing services, developing policies, undertaking community education campaigns, need to be informed by the views of children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We do things with children, not to or for children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to consider cultural and religious preference or influences and, again, to do this effectively, we need to speak with the consumer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Trauma-informed practice is an approach that recognises that trauma is common, that people accessing services may be affected by trauma and, that trauma can have a significant impact on how a person sees and interacts with the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Trauma-informed practice is an approach that is holistic, empowering, strengths-focused, collaborative and reflective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Trauma-informed practice can be individual- or service-based and it can be whole-of-community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, research suggests that exposure to nature can reduce stress and increase overall well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Finland has actively embraced this idea and their integration of nature into urban spaces has been associated with positive mental health outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential that those delivering therapeutic services are suitably qualified and regulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This was highlighted by my fellow Nominated Member of Parliament hon Dr Syed Harun.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I am sharing my perspective as an educator.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We do, however, need to recognise the invaluable assistance that suitably trained volunteers can offer to their friends, colleagues and the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Peer-to-peer support networks, particularly among young people, are an essential component of a mental health service system and should be actively encouraged, maintained and valued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: At this point, I would like to share an example of a youth-led safety and well-being initiative, developed by Public Safety and Security students at the Singapore University of Social Sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The initiative was called "ReKnew" and was established by a group of students to provide a safe space to discuss sexual abuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The group adopted an approach based on the principles of restorative justice and they established learning circles to educate and empower students to discuss difficult topics in an open and safe environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It also demonstrates that it is important that we do not over-pathologise mental health and that we do not assume that everyone who is having a bad day is having a mental health crisis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, all that is needed is someone to ask, genuinely, "Hey, are you okay?" and to care about what the person says in return.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In any discussion about mental health and well-being, it is essential to discuss the workplace, and this was also highlighted by hon Member Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore has an international reputation as being a place where people work long hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In a 2019 study of 40 cities conducted by American security solutions company, Kisi, Singapore ranked as the second-most overworked city.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The post-COVID-19 trend of working from home has not helped this situation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While flexible working arrangements have definite benefits and are preferred by many employees, working from home also comes at a cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The 2022 Cigna 360 Global Well-Being Survey showed that those currently working in a hybrid model are most likely to feel stressed and to work outside normal hours at least once a week.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Not only do employees have less time to spend with their family and friends to enjoy recreational pursuits or have real holidays, the prevailing hustle culture has had a profoundly negative impact on our mental health.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The culture of working long hours needs to change.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is a workplace hazard and needs to be treated as such by employers and employees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Employers have a duty of care, to provide a safe working environment for all employees, and reasonable working hours should be considered as one of those duties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, employees need to take responsibility to prioritise their health and well-being and to stop treating working in the evening or on weekends as something to be proud of or something that they just have to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: A collaborative effort between employees and employers will ensure a healthier and more fulfilling professional and personal life for everyone involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Employee's performance should be outcome-based, and employers should model and reward reasonable hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is a normal reaction to an abnormal or unpleasant situation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Looking back, I think it was early signs of burnout.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Luckily, I was aware of what I was going through.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I detected the signs, and I took steps to care for myself.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And I am grateful that the self-care worked.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think this is what breaking stigma is all about and needs to be about.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is about normalising the struggles and challenges that so many of us have gone through or will go through at some point in time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is about shining a light on these common experiences, deeply personal but actually common experiences, because they should not remain in the shadows of our minds and souls and we should chase these shadows away.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is about normalising the process – the journey of coping, of regaining health and well-being and of becoming better.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It will take all of us, a whole-of-society effort.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It cannot be the start of policy interventions or legislation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It takes the whole of society to talk more openly about our own mental health journeys.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Imagine a day, when parents tell their children, “Look, daddy and mummy have our struggles too, we may not fully understand yours, the struggles you are going through, but we know what it is like to be trying to cope on your own, so let’s help each other get through our challenges together.” Imagine a day when bosses and supervisors in workplaces can tell their employees, “Look, we too have bad days, please tolerate and hold space for us, just as we must for all of you and let’s work together to protect and promote mental health on our jobs”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have said this before during COS 2022, and I will say it again.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our words, our language and our actions, which shape our everyday discourse and interactions, really matter.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When we are careless with our words and actions, or worse, when we choose to deliberately exploit and weaponise mental health with our words and actions, these set all of us back.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These tear people down, they build walls back up and they set the whole of society back in our journey to eliminate stigma.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This may be a familiar name to some of us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Lisa and her father have been coming out and sharing their story about Lisa’s struggles with depression and her journey in healing and recovery.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Their story clearly resonates with others because Lisa has gathered quite a following on social media.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And, by the way, this is alongside her full-time work because Lisa is also a thriving professional.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, there are folks whom Lisa may be meeting for the first time but who already know of her and her story through social media.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Lisa tells me some of these people, meeting her for the first time have gone, “Oh, so you are the girl with depression!” To be clear, there is no ill intent behind these words.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, these words may be borne of excitement, of resonance and of gratitude to Lisa for coming out and encouraging others with her story.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And to Lisa’s credit, being the incredible person that she is, she totally took these words in her stride.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But such words, while coming from a good place, can cut quite deeply.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, we need to be aware and we need to be conscious that our words and actions really matter and we need to learn the right language.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On the other hand, when our words and actions are understanding, authentic and sensitive, it helps someone else to reach out to us.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And it can also help us to reach someone who may need our help and care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, let us build a kind, compassionate environment, a society free of stigma for mental health challenges, starting with our words and our actions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
