text: The second point I like to make is to just remind all of us, as we forge ahead in this strategy – there is so much enthusiasm and support for the strategy in this House – let us remind ourselves that those who will operationalise this strategy and those who are providing care for the mental health and well-being of others, also need care themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And they may need care in different ways.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, the professionals in healthcare, social services, education, in the Home Team and even municipal services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As we try to strengthen all of these roles as touchpoints for mental health, let us remember that they are at the frontline, they are the ones dealing with difficult cases, sometimes very raw experiences.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I recently met a gentleman working on sexual trauma cases.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I took the chance to ask if he still climbs regularly now that he is working.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: He said yes, in fact, he has to because it is his "me time" to get away from the cases that he is working with and, in his words, to “keep his sanity”.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They need care and we need to care for them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is certainly ideal for persons with mental health conditions to remain plugged into the community while coping with their conditions, but we all know that some in the community are really not coping well.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They were not coping well, they had disruptive behaviour but they were being kept in the community.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One day, my resident lost his cool and got into a physical altercation with the family members.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: He spoke to my team, and we helped him defend himself against the charges.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the point is, caregivers can break, and caregivers need care too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To summarise, as we aim to build what my hon colleague Dr Wan Rizal has described as "a next frontier in our national strategy for mental health and well-being", let us remember those professionals and caregivers standing at this new frontier and let us systematically take care of their mental health and well-being too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Let us make this a key workstream, a concerted vertical in our national strategy for mental health and well-being – caring for those who give care.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, I think insurance must play a bigger role.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But besides MediShield, I think philanthropy and charities must play a key role too.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That is the second thought I will provide here.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the past, we have had philanthropy and charities anchoring intermediate and long-term care in our healthcare landscape.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And more currently, we have philanthropy looking deep into new frontiers in our healthcare landscape, like palliative care and special needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think we need mental health to become another new and next frontier for strategic philanthropic action, for breakthrough private-public-people partnerships.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I call on all stakeholders in the space to seriously think about funding and supporting mental health, and the national strategy for mental health and well-being in a big way, as a whole-of-society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the attitudes toward the mental health, especially among younger Singaporeans, are changing, it remains a topic that many people would rather not talk about.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Much of this stigma could have arisen from two sources.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, as a society, Singapore has traditionally placed a high value on success as represented by academic achievements and/or material acquisition.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With academic achievement, you should end up being able to acquire more materially.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While these societal measures of success are slowing changing, there is still a sizeable proportion of the population that equates academic success at every level of education and having a well-paying job, a high-flying career and material acquisition as the pinnacle of accomplishments in life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Acknowledging that one is facing mental health struggles could thus be perceived as being incongruent with these societal ideals of success and be further misinterpreted as a form of weakness or failure.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, the general lack of understanding of what constitutes mental health could have led to a conflation between “mental health” and “mental disorders.” The distinction between the two, Sir, is important.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A better understanding of the differences between them could possibly be a game-changer that might help to destigmatise the conversation around mental health.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mental health refers to a state of psycho-emotional well-being where individuals can cope with normal daily stressors, being able to lead a fruitful, productive and fulfilling life.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mental disorder, on the other hand, refers to diagnosable mental condition that affects the way people think, behave, function and interact with others.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All of us probably have had mental health issues at one time or another, just like how we have all probably had issues with our physical health.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having a state of poor mental health does not necessarily mean that we have a psychiatric disorder, although persistently poor mental health over prolonged period could lead to mental disorders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is therefore important that we identify symptoms of poor mental health early and provide targeted interventions before mental health challenges progress to mental disorders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would now like to talk about the cost of poor mental health.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the World Mental Health Day 2023 Report published by Ipsos, close to half of respondents in Singapore placed mental health as the biggest healthcare challenge faced by the country today, with cancer coming in second, and stress, which is highly correlated with mental health, in third place.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Close to 50% of respondents reported being depressed to the point of feeling hopeless for weeks and roughly one-third of respondents had self-hurt and suicidal thoughts.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The same study also reported that about a quarter of respondents experienced debilitating mental health and stress-related issues that impeded their daily lives on several occasions in a year.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Close to 40% of respondents took time off from work due to mental health and stress, with 15% having done so on multiple occasions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These results correspond with a similar study published by Duke-NUS Medical School and IMH in June 2023.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What is telling from these studies is not the number of people reporting poor mental health, but the low number of people who have proactively sought interventions for their mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the reasons provided by the Ipsos study on why the treatment gap exists despite the general belief among Singaporeans that mental health is just as important as physical health, is because of the belief that the national healthcare system in Singapore does not reflect the same level of importance for mental health as it does with physical health.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Perhaps, there is a kernel of truth in this belief.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the same vein, there is only one mental hospital in Singapore, the IMH, that is serving a population of more than five million people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also a perceived social stigma of seeking treatment at IMH since IMH sees both patients experiencing mental health and mental disorders, and people tend to associate individuals seeking treatments at IMH, regardless of their underlying conditions, as “crazy” even though they might not be suffering from mental disorders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fact that IMH is colloquially referred to as “Siao Lang Keng” or the “mad house” in Hokkien is a reflection of this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The general unwillingness to acknowledge that one is experiencing mental wellness challenges in fear of being labelled as a “failure” or being perceived as “weak”, the low ratio of mental health professionals to population and social stigma of seeking interventions at IMH for mental health issues will exert and is already exerting a toll on the community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We thus need to consider the social cost of not seeking treatment for mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, not seeking early and timely intervention due to stigma and the lack of accessibility to mental healthcare will erode the human capital potential of those experiencing mental wellness issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their overall well-being and functionality could be compromised, limiting their ability to realise their full potential as well as their ability to lead a fulfilling life in the long run.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, the caregivers of those experiencing mental health challenges are likely to be their immediate family members who might not be equipped with the right knowledge to provide care.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have heard many Members already speak about this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These family members are likely to experience the stress of caregiving due to the lack of caregiving knowledge and training, possibly experiencing mental health challenges themselves in the long run.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to pay more attention to how we can better support early intervention by making structural changes to our mental health ecosystem and the wider social attitudes towards help-seeking.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, to talk about how we can enhance the mental health ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the ways to encourage individuals to seek help early is to normalise help-seeking.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will bring affordable and professionally managed interventions into workplaces instead of having companies to design their own support schemes from scratch.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the public front, a greater level of awareness must be created on what constitutes mental health and how having poor mental health or poor mental well-being is different from having a psychiatric disorder or psychiatric illness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, delinking mental health interventions from psychiatric interventions provided by IMH will further help to "de-label" and destigmatise help-seeking.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The lynchpin in the national mental healthcare plan is the number of mental healthcare professionals and the availability of caregiver support programmes in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once the numbers of mental healthcare professionals are brought up, would MOH consider setting up community-based mental wellness interventions and caregiver support programmes, perhaps, even in the polyclinics so that these resources are more widely accessible in the heartlands, leaving the proposed National Mental Wellness Centre to focus on more specialised and deeper interventions?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the issue of mental wellness has taken on greater importance and urgency.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that we are paying more attention to the issue today, and I hope that the Government and, indeed, the whole of society, will adopt a more targeted approach to promote the topic and to make mental healthcare more accessible to those who need it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I end my speech in firm support of the Motion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is aligned with the Government's National Mental Health and Well-being Strategy introduced last year.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My speech today will focus on the topic of mental wellness during and after pregnancy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I wish to share my personal experience of being in this category when I was expecting my eldest daughter.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My daughter was born five years ago, but even today, I can still remember vividly feeling delighted, yet fearful about being a first-time mom.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The lack of sleep, coupled with the stress and anxiety of raising a newborn as a rookie mom caused me to be constantly exhausted, both mentally and physically.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I was also unable to provide enough for my baby through breastfeeding alone, which intensified my feelings of guilt, sadness and frustration.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Looking back, most of the stressors I faced then actually centred around social stigmas and expectations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My own troubles with breastmilk production stemmed from the normalised expectation that all mothers should be able to provide sustenance for their children exclusively by themselves.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And like many working mothers, I also wrestled with my priorities of fulfilling my motherly duties while juggling my work obligations as a litigation lawyer, all of which contributed to much worry and stress that consequently sapped my energy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, my daughter is an active, healthy and happy child.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even so, part of me still finds it difficult to forgive myself for not being able to provide her with the best in those early days, even though I know that I had done my best then.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having gone through some difficult times during my first pregnancy, I can empathise with fellow moms who struggle with the stresses of raising their children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The experience, combined with the knowledge gained over the past few years through my interactions with fellow like-minded mommies, also helped me to prepare myself mentally for the arrival of my second bundle of joy last year, a baby boy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During my confinement following the birth of my second child, I came across news articles about fellow mothers who had died by suicide with their infant children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The stories were tragic, but they also serve as reminders about the importance of recognising every mother's mental well-being during pregnancy and throughout the months after delivery.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This result does not come as a surprise to me.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am, therefore, heartened that one of the focus areas of our national mental health strategy pertains to strengthening mental health services for pregnant women.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As we look into the well-being of mothers, I hope we may hopefully also be solving a pain point in our national birthrates.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, various hospitals in Singapore, such as the National University Hospital (NUH) and KKH, have implemented their own respective measures to identify signs of postpartum depression.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are critical initiatives to enable early detection and ensure individualised care can be given at the earliest opportunity to prevent mummies' conditions from worsening.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we will need to ensure that all hospitals in Singapore, public and private, that provide obstetrics and gynaecology services, are uniformly equipped with the relevant capabilities and resources to provide early detection and timely intervention to parents showing signs of requiring psychological support.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just as the monitoring of physical health is paramount for postpartum mums, so, too, should we devote resources to ensure their mental well-being after birth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Under the new national strategy announced last year, I note that more hospitals, polyclinics and GPs will be providing mental health services.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I hope that MOH will ensure that these services will be provided to new parents facing issues in this area to encourage them to seek help through these various avenues.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can we expect to have more polyclinics provide mental health-related services during the regular routine check-ups for the babies?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from checking and ensuring that the various milestones of the newborn are met, I propose that these trained doctors and nurses also should take the opportunity to enquire about the parents' psychological states and advise them on the help and support available should they require it.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As such, besides investing more resources in our healthcare system to improve coverage for mental wellness, I believe that we, as a community, should also band together to do our part towards increasing awareness of postpartum depression and provide a peer support network to ease the anxieties of mothers of newborn babies.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In 2021, I chanced upon an article on the Internet about Depressed Cake Shop Singapore and its founders, Debbra Lee and Tracy Heah, where they shared about their respective postpartum depression experience and how they eventually decided to set up a campaign to raise awareness in this aspect through baking or purchasing of grey cakes with a pop of colour, with grey symbolising depression and a spot of colour signifying hope.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I subsequently reached out to both of them to explore the possibility of working together to better support fellow mothers out there with their emotional well-being.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The three of us hit it off right away from our first meeting and we began discussing ideas to collaborate with the objective of sharing practical tips to restore our mental health and accumulate our mental wealth to Woodgrove residents.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Last year, in collaboration with Mumpreneurs Go Places, the PAP Women's Wing Woodgrove branch continued to reach out to our community on mental wellness through a series of workshops, with one session focusing particularly on equipping participants with tips to practise self-care amidst busy schedules between work and family care commitments.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   From pregnancy to the birth of the baby, mothers often spend a lot of effort in caring for the newborn, neglecting that they themselves have also undergone many significant changes both physically and mentally.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Postpartum depression needs to receive attention and support from society, regardless of gender.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If not treated promptly, it will not only have adverse effects on individual health, marriage, family life and career, but also affect the development of the baby. : I am thankful that throughout my two pregnancies, my husband was always by my side, providing both assistance and comfort, which he still does today.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We both believe that parenthood is a partnership of equals.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our shared experience has taught me that fathers too deserve recognition and support, and increasingly so as they got more involved in parenting.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Similarly, they also deserve the same level of emotional support as they are equally susceptible to the effects of stress and depression from parenting-related causes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am heartened to know that there are many who share the same opinion.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With that said, social stereotypes that push men towards the supposed ideal image of a strong, uncomplaining individual do exist, thus discouraging them from openly sharing emotions and getting support for depression.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While that affects the mental well-being of men in general, it is more pronounced for fathers who would have to grapple with even more pressing worries and doubts.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, one way to improve support for our fathers is to reduce the social stigma of men seeking emotional help, whether through friends and family, or via professional counselling services.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By reassuring dads that seeking a listening ear is permitted and even encouraged, we can do much to improve their emotional and mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Much has been said in recent years about the benefits of remote working in terms of achieving work-life balance, but it may be worth more of exploring an expanded version of remote working, especially for dads to cope with the arrival of their newborn and further ease the transition from paternity leave to resuming normal duties at work.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, the topic of mental health has increasingly become a serious issue both in Singapore and around the world.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I applaud our Government for their foresight in focusing on this area, as lack of issues and action will lead to even more widespread problems in Singapore in the future, economically, socially and security-wise.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By tackling these issues head on, we will be able to ensure that Singaporeans will be further equipped to weather the storms as one united people.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has been widely discussed by fellow Parliamentarians today, reflecting a societal shift towards greater openness and our concerted effort and action on this issue.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I will focus my speech on the call for whole-of-Singapore effort to implement this strategy of promoting the mental health and well-being of two particular groups of people – seniors staying alone and senior caregivers in our community, and on improving workplace mental health and well-being.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On promoting the mental health and well-being of seniors staying alone and senior caregivers in the community, we need to work on de-medicalising and normalising conversations surrounding mental health, increase mental health literacy and improve societal attitudes and reduce stigma towards individuals with mental health needs, as mentioned by many of fellow Parliamentarians today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond policies and Ministry effort, we need the wider community to have the right knowledge and understanding about mental health conditions that will aid their recognition, management or prevention.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes the ability to recognise symptoms of mental health conditions and to know where to seek help.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, it becomes increasingly important to strengthen the informal support networks in the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last Friday, I met Mdm Tan during our house visit.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She shared with me how difficult it was to be caring for her own mother when she herself was getting older.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But she said with a smile, "As hard as it is, it is my duty as she is my mother".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of our other residents, Mdm Elena, is herself in her mid-60s.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She has no siblings and is not married.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She is taking care of her two elderly parents; her father in his 90s goes to the daily dementia care home and her mother, who is in her 80s, has dementia and stays at home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another one of our residents, Mr Aziz, is a kidney dialysis patient in his 70s and taking care of his mother with dementia, who is in her 90s.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are many individuals like Mdm Tan, Mdm Elena and Mr Aziz who are retirees but themselves caring for their parents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Caregivers can undergo an immense amount of stress, what more when the caregivers themselves are dealing with their own challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond policies from MOH, how can the community come together to support individuals like this better?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Pasir Ris, our community volunteers through our Pasir Ris East care store, visit the families every third Saturday of the month to catch up with them and check on how they are doing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For Mdm Elena, some of the grassroots leaders, such as Mr Charlie Cheong, offer to care for her parents while she gets a haircut, goes to the market or takes the day off from caregiving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we continue to encourage more from the community to come forward and provide assistance to support the mental burden of such caregivers, especially in our fast-ageing society?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To borrow the words of fellow MP Mariam Jaafar in her speech earlier, "We must care more for each other in our society." Secondly, on improving workplace mental health and well-being, we know that good work is beneficial for our mental health.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A healthy state of mental well-being can also contribute to improved productivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While companies can also put in policies to prevent workplace discrimination in their organisation and to prevent the discrimination for mental health and encourage mental well-being at the workplace, translating these strategies into practice poses significant challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, how do managers manage conversations and, in particular, performance appraisals, as it is the season now, for colleagues or subordinates with mental health conditions without making them feel discriminated, especially if their performance is affected by it when compared to other peers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we then balance and manage the expectation with the rest of the team too?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But the devil is in the details when we try to translate the intent into practice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we want the approach towards mental health to change in the workplace, employers, employees and the people leaders must be equipped with the right skillset to drive that change.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should that skillset be made available as a guideline for employees on the "do"s and the "don’t"s or should we impose it as a legal requirement by MOM?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I would first like to declare myself and my interest as a self-employed transformative and healing coach.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are three points I wish to highlight about mental health to contribute to our collective understanding of it so that we can properly contemplate what this means to our nation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: By framing mental health as just a healthcare challenge, we risk adopting the traditional language of health, which pathologises and creates a chronic reliance on only formal healthcare institutions and medication.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This relegates the ownership of recovery to the field of experts, such as psychologists and psychiatrists, which are in very short supply and also renders the individual dependent on the formal healthcare system’s capacity, which has its limitations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mental health is something that every person can own, and be equipped to take care of for ourselves, until it deteriorates to a point where clinical assistance is necessary and that is where clear navigation and adequate resourcing of expert and clinical interventions are important.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But I urge us to think and to go one step further, to also equip individuals.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can encourage a wide variety of activities that are personal-based to help Singaporeans access knowledge for maintaining their mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are activities such as yoga and meditation, as our colleague Mr Darryl David said, mindfulness practices, and different forms of traditional, art-based, music-based and somatic-based approaches to mental, emotional and spiritual wellness, which are all available currently, although relegated as "alternative wellness".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is time, I say, to mainstream these options because they are derived from the rich and deep history, wisdom and heritage of our Asian cultures.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: They cater to the varied cultural, faith and spiritual beliefs of Singaporeans and offer individuals more options towards holistic wellness that are accessible, and which resonate with each individual’s inclinations and preferences.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will accelerate and propagate emotional wellness skills more widely so that everyone can equip themselves to maintain good mental health as a lifelong endeavour.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Mental health, just like physical health, is a journey that requires daily awareness and maintenance, starting with emotional literacy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can do its part to help make such knowledge and training more ubiquitous and accessible for the common man and woman on the street.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And here, I would like to share an example on what happens when I go to my training workshops.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As a facilitator, I often ask the participants: "How are you feeling now?" And often, the replies I get are "Okay lor" or "Like that lor".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It tells me that Singaporeans are sorely lacking in the emotional vocabulary to be able to identify and even acknowledge our own emotions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: One key point I would like to make, most importantly, is let us recognise the invisible forces that are undoing our mental health and mental health efforts.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What is the invisible force that is taking our attention away from something that all of us agree to be important, so important that we have a Motion in this Chamber today?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Our attitude towards stress at work illustrates this.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What is illuminating is that despite acknowledging its intentions, there were many concerns over its feasibility.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For example, would bosses and other colleagues see a desire for greater work-life balance as a sign of lower motivation compared to their peers competing for the same limited opportunities?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What happened to the age-old wisdom, in Chinese, “休息是为了走更长远的路”, meaning "Rest is to help us travel even further"?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How have we, as a society, come to equate rest with lower motivation?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What has caused this collective judgement that demonises the act of rest and restoration?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In a recent commentary on CNA by NUS lecturer Jonathan Sim, he talks about youth "hustle culture" and warns of the perils of a lack of the ability to introspect.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: He observed that, for many university students, introspection is sidelined as a, I quote, "stagnant inactivity" because pausing to do it "does not seem to contribute directly to any measurable progress".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: He notes, and I quote, "the inability to sit alone with their thoughts and the tendency to bury themselves in work or digital distractions, creating a superficial busyness that masks an inability to process deeper emotions".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This does not just afflict youths, but many successful adults as well, including many of us in the Chamber.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In my role as a healing coach, I have come across many accomplished professionals and leaders who baulk at the idea of slowing down.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Are we somehow living within a bubble where a constant need to be achieving something has made slowing down something that terrifies people?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The term "stress-laxing" is found in UrbanDictionary.com, feeling stressed because you are relaxing and not working, the cause of your stress in the first place!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We have to recognise what is creating this "pressure cooker" bubble we are all living in.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The very narrative of our nation's survival and success thus far has been fuelled by the notion of scarcity which then fuels an endless culture of competition and a sense of inadequacy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This is, unintentionally, of course, encapsulated by our classic National Day song "Stand Up for Singapore." If you recall the lyrics, we are first called to stand up for Singapore to do the "best you can", only to be called a few lines later to also "be prepared to give a little more." I love this song.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I love to sing it with pride and increasingly, I recognise, some irony.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Are we perhaps the only country in the world where our best is still not enough?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To be clear, I am not calling for slackness because reaching our fullest potential does require hard work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am also not a proponent of the "lie flat" movement either.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I am trying to solve or prevent it.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Learning from hypercompetitive Asian societies, like South Korea and China where the 躺平, or "lie flat" movement has begun as a silent rebellion by youths against a system in which many feel hopeless about ever catching up with, we must be mindful of the long-term costs of a "pressure cooker" society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can see this already happening when new technology emerges, such as AI, what a helpful tool, to help us be more productive.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But instead of working less, we end up cramping more expectations into our workplans to achieve even more.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What is stopping us from reaping the benefits and advantages of technology to avail ourselves the precious time to rest, to nurture relationships and to enjoy our families?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: An economically prosperous yet chronically unhealthy Singapore would be a hollow success.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In an individual, chronic stress and tension entrenches the flight or fight response as a default reaction.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In an ecosystem, chronic stress entrenches similar responses, such as demanding, defending, deflecting or sometimes, a collective numbing, which manifests as a lack of ownership.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This may hurt to hear but our Civil Service is one of the most afflicted.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I do not blame our civil servants because they take the brunt of overwhelming workloads that inadvertently cause mental and emotional burnout.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We surely must agree that a burnt-out and emotionally "checked out" people is not what will create progress.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The inability to slow down is a serious symptom that we are disregulated as an ecosystem and society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We must take daring steps to foster a collective restoration of our societal nervous system.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The "Right to Disconnect" has to be seen as a necessity, not as a problematic "nice-to-have".

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Do we have the gumption to allow a collective slowing down, to cater time and space for our collective mental and emotional restoration?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It may sound illogical or even terrifying to some, to cater for a period of slowing down, especially when imagined in economic terms.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But I challenge the notion that growth and productivity is only possible with relentless hard work, especially in this technologically abundant era.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Growth is possible with more collaboration in place of competition.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This office should consist of well-being champions from each Ministry and Statutory Board, and include a consultative committee of representatives from the private and people sectors.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Their role can be as resource persons, sounding boards as well as act as inter-Ministry bridgers to ensure the well-being lens is present in policy discussions and formulation across Ministries.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will actualise what Singaporeans have already expressed in many Forward SG conversations, that desire for a different vision for Singapore, in the paths available, the aspirations and the definitions of success.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans want to thrive, without being in a constant rat race.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How might we enable a deeper sense of fulfilment than the never-ending chasing of KPIs, material or financial success?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It tells us that the answer lies in the intangibles, the quality of our relationships with ourselves, with the people around us, as well as with our planet earth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This aspect of life requires a slowing down introspection in order to be nurtured.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If slowing down feels foreign, selfish or even un-Singaporean, we can seek inspiration from our National Pledge.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such sense of security and satisfaction is critical to mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Let us focus on our abundance and on an attitude of gratitude to foster the collective sense of security.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What do we wish to see in our children's and youths' faces?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly not stress, not anxiety or the blank disconnected faces like what we are seeing increasingly today, afflicted and glazed over by digital addictions, anti-depressants or sleeping aids that they use to cope with the disconnection within them untended to and unheld by our collective lack of mindful presence and the constant doubting of what is enough.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It also indicated that the rise in suicide rates was the highest amongst the elderly and the young.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was a perturbing figure and I have come across more than one case of residents affected by suicide.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The cases of two teenagers were particularly sad.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In one case, I spoke to the parents who were utterly devastated, saying they could not understand how their daughter who appeared to be a well-behaved and obedient child, suddenly decided to take her own life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In another case, I heard from a young resident whose best friend decided to take her own life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The friend was utterly devasted by this and had to deal with depression herself.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first is, whether these people had undetected mental health issues, including depression and/or the inability to deal with some difficult or stressful situation the person was facing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second is whether, even if such issues were detected, the interventions to deal with them were adequate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Based on the response provided by the Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary at that time, it did seem like this was a matter that the Ministry was taking seriously.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I do have some further clarifications and suggestions in this regard.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to the clarifications, it will be helpful if the Government is able to share how it tracks the effectiveness of its outreach programmes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, do the HPB's programmes targeted at parents reach all parents?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Do the HPB and NCSS' campaigns, targeted at encouraging people to get help, reach their intended audience?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One way to gauge this would be if we can identify whether, of the people who ultimately committed suicide, there was a way to track whether any of these programmes had reached them?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second is to track the effectiveness of the interventions once people come forward to ask for help.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For this, an important statistic would be tracking how many of those who had committed suicide had come forward to seek assistance and were, therefore, "known" cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that the main intervention for those seeking assistance now is administered by social service agencies at the community level.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, dealing with people with suicidal tendencies is a complex matter and where, for example, there may be underlying conditions, such as depression, there may be a need for professional intervention from psychologists or psychiatrists.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will be particularly important for, say, students or the elderly who may wish to seek assistance but may be concerned about whether they have the means to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A related aspect of this is to encourage insurance policies to cover or provide for mental health assistance as a rider.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the largest increase in suicides was amongst the elderly and young, the largest number is still amongst the working adult population.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, in workplaces, it may also be useful to have such access to mental health assistance for employees as a benefit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In many European countries and the United States (US), for example, companies have an Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) where employees can seek assistance for mental health issues on a confidential basis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As this is provided by employers, the costs of doing this can generally be aggregated over a large pool of employees.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I should declare that my mother is a psychologist who currently provides EAP services to several companies and this was where I actually learnt about this service from.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Her end-customers are generally multinational companies who offer EAP as an employee benefit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The consultations with the psychologists are confidential, so the employees do not have to worry about stigma in seeking assistance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I understand that employees come forward with a wide range of issues, from dealing with family breakdowns to coping with the fear of retrenchment exercises when companies go through such exercises.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both scenarios are generally traumatic for people and they also bring with them financial insecurity for the employees, which may make them reluctant to seek assistance privately.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In these scenarios, having an employment benefit that gives them access to professional mental health assistance, in this case, trained psychologists or counsellors, can make a huge difference.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Government with their national-level programmes, such as Healthier SG, National Mental Health and Well-Being Strategy, ground mobilisation of more general practitioners (GPs) and increasing capacity for medical psychiatric care, has indeed given importance and priority in this matter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, if our nation is a tapestry, mental health is the thread that weaves through every level of our nation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is not about unique issues but about solutionings that are always nuanced and personal.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I put it to the House that complementing our national initiatives must be a network of localised support comprising of energised outreach, awareness and authentic friendships.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, ground-up initiatives are invaluable as they address, in a spot-on manner, mental health issues faced by real individuals whilst rallying the support and understanding of real-life neighbours in the communities we all live in.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They are out of the national system of care, as they were simply never registered in the system in the first place.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some lead quiet, isolated lives, depending on neighbours and the Residents' Committees to keep a discreet watch on their well-being.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some lead more colourful lives and are called unkindly, sometimes, as weird and strange.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet there are some, who are fully dependent on their caregivers, many of whom, are sole caregivers who have given up their lives and livelihoods to take care of their wards.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These families living in our midst are often stressed, worried and financially challenged.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I met Mr Tan and his sister, not their real names, about two years ago, when there was a fire in their block.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Both were in their 50s and despite the fire, Ms Tan refused to be evacuated.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ms Tan later shared that she suspects that her brother has special needs and is a recluse as he refuses to leave their home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After their parents passed away, she stopped work and became his full-time caregiver.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She is frustrated about the situation and worried about what will become of her brother if something happens to her.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She told me that she would rather die in the fire at home, with her brother, than go through the trauma of forcing her brother to leave the house, climb down the stairs and wait at the fire refuge area with strangers while waiting for the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) to give the all-clear.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While both the Tans were physically unharmed in the fire, the state of their mental wellness calls for care and support.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to do more for families like the Tans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Local support can certainly alleviate some of the stress and loneliness, be it the reassuring familiarity of neighbours checking in on you or participating in nearby community events.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in order for local support to be effective and inclusive, the community needs awareness and specialised training.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Most of our Resident Networks now have a volunteer leader with higher awareness of mental health issues, especially those faced by caregivers and their senior or special needs wards.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has impacted the way we organise our community events and conduct our home visits.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We hope to scale our local training, as we believe that more volunteers and the community-at-large would benefit from such training and awareness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the same thread, livelihoods are a major contributor to mental wellness and, for caregivers, jobs in the community are always warmly welcomed for better work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can more be done by our local merchants on local job creation?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we encourage and equip our heartland merchants to embrace flexible work arrangements (FWA), especially with the upcoming Tripartite Guidelines for FWA requests?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How about our local Community Development Councils (CDCs) promoting local job creation and FWAs with the heartland merchant networks that they have created so successfully with the CDC Voucher programmes?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With tailwinds helping along in the creation of livelihood opportunities for our caregivers, let us seize the moment and secure a peace of mind for our caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Support for the mental health of our caregivers is a multifaceted one – providing support and respite in the care for their wards, creating caregiver support groups and the providence of local jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Local stakeholders and the organisation of our local stakeholders are critical in sustainable mental health support.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, this is where ground-level initiatives, like the Positivity Pizza Movement, become invaluable.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Led by the youths for our youths in Punggol Shore, this movement promotes mental well-being in our youth community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our community's way of telling our youths that it is okay not to be okay and the whole Punggol Shore Community has our youths' backs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The inspiration for the movement was at an encounter I had with a young Punggol resident.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: C, not her real name, came up to me when I was doing my regular rounds at a local mall.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we were speaking, C saw a keychain plushie I had on my bag and she said, "Ms Yeo, that's really very cute.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When initiatives like the Positivity Pizza movement are driven by the people who care about and understand the dynamics of their own community, supported by the warmth of common shared spaces, there is a profound authenticity that connects with residents on a very personal level.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These localised efforts tap into the values, traditions and shared experiences of the community, fostering a sense of belonging and collective responsibility.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This age group is particularly vulnerable as it accounts for 13% of the global burden.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In fact, based on the Mental Health Foundation, 10% of children and young people from age five to 16 have a clinically diagnosed mental problem.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Yet, 70% of children and adolescents who experienced mental health problems have not had appropriate interventions at a sufficiently early age.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Even if we take a conservative approach and with all estimates, take a discount and assume one out of eight instead of one out of seven.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The number for those who are undiagnosed will be far greater.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It would probably be one out of seven or one out of six, a value closer to those reporting countries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The global statistics for suicide amongst children and adolescents show that, every year, 47,000 end their own lives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Suicide is the most tragic outcome of a mental health condition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: However, anything short of that, the consequences of failing to address children and adolescents' mental health conditions will extend to adulthood, impairing both physical and mental health and limiting opportunities to lead fulfilling lives as adults.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is the problem definition that we are facing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The question is: do we have the resources to manage mental health challenges?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and dopamine are two critical neurotransmitters in the brain that play significant roles in regulating various physiological and psychological processes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, which helps to calm down nerve activity, reducing neural excitability throughout the nervous system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Dopamine, on the other hand, is a neurotransmitter that is involved in reward, motivation, memory, attention and even regulating body movements.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The levels of activity of these neurotransmitters can change over time due to various factors, including age, stress, environmental influences and hormonal changes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, to put it simply, if you are driving, you can view dopamine as the accelerator and GABA as the brakes – both essential and both countering and balancing the needs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But as children approach puberty, it is marked by significant changes in hormones, including increases in estrogen and testosterone.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These hormones have been shown to influence GABA neurotransmission.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For example, estrogen can modulate GABA receptor expression and function, potentially altering the efficacy of GABAergic inhibition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Testosterone has been implicated in the modulation of GABAA receptors, which might inhibit signalling.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: During puberty, the brain undergoes substantial restructuring and pruning of neural connections.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The maturation of neural circuits, especially in the prefrontal cortex and limbic system, involves changes in the balance between excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmission.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As the brain rewires itself for adult functioning, as part of puberty, the role and regulation of GABA may shift, leading to a temporal reduction in inhibitory effects on the neural circuits.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Members must be wondering why I am highlighting these evolving conditions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is important because it is a critical period.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, puberty also coincides with the most critical period of neuroplasticity, where the brain is particularly sensitive to environmental inputs and experiences.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The changes in GABA transmission during this time may reflect the brain's adaptation to these inputs, altering synaptic strength and connectivity in a way that requires modification of inhibitory signalling.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This also means that the brain is developing, forming and setting the foundations of its neurochemical activity which may have a long-lasting impact throughout life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, imagine being a child or an adolescent having to manage these changes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is made more difficult because the change is not overnight.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is a gradual but relatively rapid change, which requires a keen sense of self-awareness and learning how to self-manage and respond.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is a swirl of changing chaos for a young individual.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, imagine those who grew up driving an automatic transmission all their lives and, suddenly, in a short period of time, they have to learn and drive a manual transmission but with an additional complication that the sensitivity of the accelerator, brakes and clutch is constantly changing.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Imagine how many times the engine would have grinded to a halt and having to learn and restart again.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Given all these, we have yet to include the environmental influences, genetic factors and adverse experiences, such as abuse, neglect, exposure to violence, exposure to adversity, pressure to conform with peers and the exploration of identity, quality of home life and relationships with peers, bullying, harsh parenting and socio-economic problems.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is no longer a simple scenario of travelling or driving along an expressway.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Imagine being caught in a traffic jam within the car park at Plaza Singapura on a weekend.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: You are going up a spiral slope on the next level.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: You are a newly minted driver, driving a manual transmission vehicle with constantly changing accelerator and brakes and clutch.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: A sequence of clutch, brake, gear, brake, accelerator, clutch, accelerator, brake.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be where the help is needed, where the children and adolescents are.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our student councillors are managing an overwhelming caseload.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our student welfare officers are working in parallel.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Teachers trained in counselling are doing their level best, juggling the multiple hats and roles.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our child protective services caseloads will need more capacity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But we need to get the required help to those in the moderate and mild risk levels to prevent further escalation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Family Service Centres (FSCs) with counsellors and psychologists are leaning forward and assisting schools and families in need.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Guidance branch and psychological service branches are working hard on the cases.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We need specialists that have deep skills to manage cases, such as the "hidden youth syndrome", which is also known as hikikomori.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These are much lower than the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is not uncommon to wait for two to three months for a diagnosis, whilst the child continues to lose time in school, stacking on the challenges further.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our methodology and the typical observe, orient, decide and act (OODA) framework, though still relevant, will be less effective here.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Each year, we are looking at a mass transition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Some will face greater difficulty and others less.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We should not leave it to chance because the transition is a 100% certainty of occurrence.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But how it is navigated will have less certain outcomes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, let us sharpen our emphasis and target resources on this specific transition to ensure that all our kids have a more certain outcome.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the spirit of KidSTART, where we are rooted in the belief that every child deserves a strong start in life, regardless of their socio-economic background, this guiding principle is embodied in KidSTART's comprehensive approach to supporting early childhood development for children from low-income families.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is designed to ensure that these children have access to the same opportunities for healthy development as their peers, recognising the profound impact that the early years on a child's future health, well-being and educational achievement.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: KidSTART celebrates its 10th anniversary and, likewise, we should do the same for our children's mental health transition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I suggest establishing a national mental health and transition programme for kids and adolescents.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: KidsSoar, a progamme that is dedicated and focused on mental health transitions for children and adolescents, which is a certainty, embodies a philosophy centred around understanding, supporting and nurturing emotional and psychological well-being of young individuals, to be pre-emptive, preventative and, if needed, resourced to support recovery.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This programme should be designed to acknowledge the importance of mental health as a critical component of overall health and to ensure that children and adolescents are equipped to navigate life's challenges with resilience, a programme that is compassionate and understanding, that empowers, through education and practice, inclusive and accessible, and holistic in approach.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This will reflect the spirit of our unwavering commitment to the growth and healing of young minds.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It acknowledges that the journey may be long and challenging, but we believe in the potential for growth, healing and positive change.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must do more, and we must do more today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In a world that often moves at an overwhelming pace, there are struggles of the mind that can be as debilitating as those of the body.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There lies a group of unsung heroes dedicated to the art and science of healing not just the individual, but the very fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This tribute is a salute to their unwavering commitment, their compassion and the profound impact they have made on the lives of those they touch.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Their work often goes beyond the call of duty.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With every individual they help, they weave a stronger and more compassionate fabric for our society, ensuring that no one has to walk the path of mental challenges alone.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They see beyond the stigma and labels, reaching out to the person struggling in the shadows, offering them a lifeline, a listening ear and the promise of a brighter tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In times of crisis, their calm and steady presence provides the anchor many need to weather their personal storms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They remind us that it is okay to be not okay and that seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Their work is a testament to the idea that mental health is an integral part of overall health, deserving of the same attention, care and respect.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Let this tribute be a reminder of the gratitude and respect that they so richly deserve.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Their dedication, patience and compassion light the way forward for all of us, as we strive towards a future where mental wellness is prioritised and cherished.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To those who are stuck in traffic on a slope with a manual transmission, fear not.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are here with you on this journey.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For me, with sincere appreciation and a grateful heart, I give thanks and tribute to all those who have taught me how to drive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: May our children soar to greater heights to the moon and beyond and above all their mighty things.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mental health has grown in importance, both in Singapore and across the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the past, people dealt with mental health issues privately.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It was always in the shadows and not something we talk about publicly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In recent times, attitudes have shifted, for the better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: People are more informed about mental health and more willing to talk about this openly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: COVID-19 also brought mental health issues to the forefront.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because across the world, people had to cut back social interactions and isolate themselves from family and friends.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And this took a toll on mental health.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The work of the Taskforce builds on previous national efforts to improve the quality and accessibility of mental health services in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will now translate these plans into action.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To understand the approach in this new strategy, we must, first, appreciate the full range of mental health issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On one end of the spectrum are mental health issues that require medical treatment, like bipolar disorder and schizophrenia.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These conditions can be debilitating, severely affecting a person's ability to carry out important daily activities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the other end of the spectrum are issues affecting mental well-being, like anxiety and stress.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: While these typically do not require medicalisation, it does not mean that we should take them lightly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If not addressed well, poor mental well-being can also affect our ability to lead our lives productively.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because mental health issues lie on a spectrum, it means we need a broad suite of solutions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Not all mental health issues need to be treated in a specialist healthcare institution.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is the same when we have a physical ailment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We do not go to a specialist for treatment immediately when we experience some symptoms of ill-health.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If it is more serious, the matter gets referred to specialist care.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, improving mental health is not just about hiring more psychiatrists or building more capacity at IMH.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we also need to strengthen capabilities across our entire spectrum of care, including at our polyclinics and GPs and across other settings, like schools, workplaces and in the community, so that more timely support can be rendered to those in need.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In our strategy, we are redoubling our efforts to better understand the issues that young people face, something that many Members spoke about.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has never been easy to be a teenager.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Teenage angst has always been part of the growing up process.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Teenagers have to learn about themselves, take on new responsibilities and prepare for adulthood.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since around the early 2010s, because the current generation of young people are expressing more concerns about their mental health than previous cohorts, many countries have reported increases in suicidal ideation as well as mental health conditions, like anxiety, and depression, amongst their youths.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Last year, the US Surgeon-General called the increasing mental health needs of US youths as the "defining public health crisis of our time".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even the Nordic countries, consistently ranking high in global happiness and well-being surveys, they, too, are reporting rises in youth anxiety, depression and a variety of mental illnesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we see a similar trend in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not at the same high levels as some other countries, where the mental health issues are conflated with other difficult issues, like drug abuse, homelessness and street violence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it is, nevertheless, a worrying trend and we are taking it seriously.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we are linking up with researchers from around the world to try and understand the root causes behind this recent surge in youth mental health issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some think that heavy social media usage is a major cause.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, the constant pressure to present a positive image online, the fear of missing out, the algorithms that flood news feeds with stories that are designed to spark outrage and the issues of cyber-bullying.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All these can take a toll on one's mental health.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, the more time spent on the Internet or social media means more sleep deprivation, less physical exercise and less real-life interactions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All of which are important for healthy brain development at a young age.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But other researchers think that there is more to it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That it is not just about more online safeguards, that we also need to loosen up in the real world and give our children more space for free play and autonomy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Because when children have less room to play and explore or to interact and build social skills at an early age, they are also less likely to grow up with the sense of independence and confidence to take charge of their own lives.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The bottom line is that more work will need to be done to better understand what has changed globally in recent years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is an area that requires further research and study to identify the key causal factors and the interplay between the factors, so that we can design and put in place appropriate interventions, based on data and evidence, to better help our young people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will equip and train an additional 28,000 frontline personnel and volunteers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They serve across our community and social service touchpoints, so they can identify people struggling with mental health and offer early assistance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) is on track to achieving its target of deploying more than 1,000 teacher-counsellors across our schools.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is on top of the basic counselling skills that all teachers will be trained in as well as the one to two counsellors that every school will have to support students with more challenging social and emotional needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will provide parents with resources to support their children's mental health and well-being needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will establish more peer support networks in the community, including in schools, institutes of higher learning (IHLs), workplaces and amongst our national servicemen.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These networks will have trained peer leaders who can spread the message on the importance of mental health and provide a first-line response to their friends or colleagues who need help.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: My colleagues, Senior Parliamentary Secretaries Rahayu Mahzam and Eric Chua, Minister of State Gan Siow Huang and Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary, will elaborate later on some of these areas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They will require more coordinated efforts across the Government – more training, people and, ultimately, Government spending.
